articles.title_orig: Matan Kahana Elected Speaker of Israel’s Parliament
articles.title_zh: Matan Kahana Elected Speaker of Israel’s Parliament
articles.content_orig:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s grip on power suffered a critical blow on Tuesday as parliament voted to elect a new speaker, giving the opposition greater control over the legislative agenda.
The Knesset elected Matan Kahana of Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party as its 26th speaker, replacing Amir Ohana, from Netanyahu’s Likud party. Kahana received the support of 66 lawmakers, according to the Knesset spokesperson.
Lawmakers voted separately on the candidates, rather than in a head-to-head ballot. Likud’s candidate, coalition whip Ofir Katz, received the support of 52 lawmakers in a separate vote.
The vote marks the first significant move by the Eisenkot-led bloc to set a new direction for the legislature since Netanyahu lost his Knesset majority in the October 27 elections. The prime minister and his coalition of right-wing and ultra-Orthodox parties won only 53 seats in the 120-seat parliament. The opposition holds 67 seats, including 48 across four Jewish parties and a record 19 for two Arab parties: the Joint List and Raam.
Eisenkot, who was tasked by President Isaac Herzog earlier this month with forming the next government, has up to four and a half more weeks to replace Netanyahu, but his path to power remains difficult. However, his bloc now controls the Knesset plenum, key positions, and legislative agenda, and plans to use them to scrutinize and constrain Netanyahu’s caretaker government, which remains in office until it is replaced.
Eisenkot said Tuesday that Kahana’s appointment is a “proper democratic move which reflects the absolute majority who voted for change.”
Eisenkot’s bloc has already appointed interim chairs for key Knesset committees, including finance and defense, expanding oversight and control over the budget and strategic affairs. Avigdor Liberman, the leader of the opposition Yisrael Beitenu party now chairing the Foreign Affairs and Defense Committee, has already said he would summon all the security chiefs for briefings.
One of the opposition’s top legislative priorities is to undo judicial overhauls from Netanyahu’s outgoing coalition that sparked unprecedented nationwide protests in 2023. Critics of the overhaul said it weakened Israel’s democratic institutions and judicial oversight of the government.
Special committees have already been established to repeal a bill that changed how judges were selected and legislation that limits and weakens the attorney general. A separate committee was formed to undo a media regulation overhaul which expanded government control over the communications and news sector. Eisenkot’s bloc has also pledged to advance the establishment of a state commission of inquiry into the failures that led to the Hamas-led attack on October 7, 2023, which Netanyahu has refused to investigate.
Netanyahu and his allies tried to block Kahana’s election and to delegitimize it as dependent on the support of the Arab parties, even though they themselves have repeatedly sought support from Arab lawmakers in parliament. During the vote, members of Netanyahu’s bloc shouted “shame” at each Arab lawmaker who voted in support of Kahana.
Likud condemned the outcome after the vote, calling it “a low point in the history of the Knesset” and saying Kahana had been elected with the votes of what it called “terror supporters.”
While Eisenkot and his allies have seized control of the Knesset, his plan to replace Netanyahu still faces significant obstacles. Eisenkot wanted to form what he calls a “national emergency government,” a minority government made of the four Jewish opposition parties, which together hold 48 seats. The Arab parties would stay out of the coalition but would guarantee a majority in the Knesset to keep the government from collapsing in exchange for various concessions.
But other leaders in Eisenkot’s bloc are pushing in different directions. Liberman has vetoed any government that relies on the Arab parties’ support and is pushing for talks with the two ultra-Orthodox parties, Shas and United Torah Judaism (UTJ), which have been traditionally allied with Netanyahu.
UTJ, the Ashkenazi ultra-Orthodox party, declined to recommend Netanyahu for the premiership in the post-election consultations and has opened the door to informal talks with Eisenkot’s bloc. But it did not support Kahana in the vote for speaker of the Knesset, instead supporting Likud’s candidate. The second ultra-Orthodox party, Shas, remains loyal to Netanyahu, leaving Liberman’s strategy uncertain.
Another obstacle is former prime minister Naftali Bennett, who reportedly favors talks on a unity government with Netanyahu’s Likud party over an alliance with the Arab or ultra-Orthodox parties. However, Netanyahu has conditioned any talks on him remaining prime minister, which Eisenkot has rejected, raising doubts Bennett’s vision can succeed.

articles.title_orig: Isolated Brazilian tribe emerges amid alarm over threats to group’s way of life
articles.title_zh: Isolated Brazilian tribe emerges amid alarm over threats to group’s way of life
articles.content_orig:
Indigenous Awá people of Amazon make contact with villagers and accept food to take back to territory
About 20 Indigenous people emerged from isolation in Brazil’s Amazon rainforest , several organizations reported on Tuesday, raising the alarm about increased invasions into the tribe’s territory.
According to the NGO Survival International, members of the Awá people, who live in voluntary isolation, arrived on Monday in a village and made contact with a government team in a “historic encounter”.
The village they entered was within the Arariboia Indigenous territory in the north-eastern state of Maranhão, home to the Guajajara ethnic group.
Local community leaders said the villagers offered food to the group.
“They asked for yams and took them back into their forest,” said Survival International.
The NGO explained that the Awá typically subsist on hunting and gathering. However, they have faced increased incursions from illegal loggers, hunters and cattle ranchers.
A video of the encounter, filmed by Guajajara villagers and released by Survival International, shows a group of men, women and children at the edge of the forest.
Partially concealed by vegetation, they appear naked and are wearing necklaces. The men carry bows and long arrows.
“The physical condition of some members, particularly the children and the elderly, caused concern among the villagers, who noted clear signs of severe emaciation,” warned Coapima, an organization representing Indigenous groups in Maranhão.
Coapima highlighted the risks that unplanned contact poses to such groups, noting that they are particularly “exposed to diseases” against which they have little to no immunity.
Funai, the public agency responsible for Indigenous affairs, said in a statement sent to AFP that its technical teams were closely monitoring the situation and analyzing available information regarding the group’s health.
Survival International’s director, Caroline Pearce, said the group’s choice to emerge from isolation was a “troubling indication of how the continued invasion of uncontacted peoples’ forests puts otherwise self-sufficient Indigenous people in real danger”.
She said the Awá were being driven into “an ever-smaller island of the Amazon rainforest, surrounded by destruction”.
According to the NGO, about 196 “uncontacted” peoples and groups, who choose to live in isolation, have been identified across 10 countries.
More than 90% of such groups live in the Amazon rainforest, primarily in Brazil , with others in Indonesia and India.
The Forest Guardians – a group of Guajajara people who have battled illegal invasions for years – warned in comments in the Survival International statement that “climate change, fires, deforestation and land encroachment” were affecting the Awá’s way of life.
According to Survival International, many of the guardians have lost their lives trying to protect the territory they share with the Awá.

articles.title_orig: Apple confirms iCloud outage as users report issues with Apple Pay, App Store and other services
articles.title_zh: Apple confirms iCloud outage as users report issues with Apple Pay, App Store and other services
articles.content_orig:
Several Apple services suffered an outage today, preventing some users from signing into iCloud and using other Apple services. According to Downdetector , a site that tracks reports of online service outages, iCloud, Apple Support, Apple Pay, and the App Store all saw spikes in reports.
Apple's support page initially indicated issues with iCloud accounts and sign-ins, as well as other services. As of 3:52 p.m. ET, services appeared to be recovering, though the support page still showed some small issues.
According to Downdetector reports, these are the services that saw spikes in outage reports:
"Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning," an Apple spokesperson told us in a statement. "We're working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible."
In addition to iCloud, Apple's support page also flags that AppleCare on Device, which lets you purchase AppleCare on your phone or tablet, is experiencing an outage. That's alongside Apple Business, Apple School Manager, iCloud Mail, iCloud Web Apps and Schoolwork
As of 1:10 p.m. ET, the page also listed the App Store and Apple Music as experiencing an outage. Around 1:41 p.m. ET, the affected services on Downdetector started showing a downward trend in reports, indicating they may be recovering.
Users online reported being signed out of services and unable to sign back in. Others reported being unable to activate new iPhones.
The issues follow a string of outages that have plagued online services over the past week. On Nov. 12, Microsoft Outlook and Teams were knocked out for more than 30 hours due to what Microsoft described as a technical issue. On Nov. 13, a technical issue caused all air traffic across the U.S. to be grounded , leading to thousands of canceled and delayed flights.
On Monday, online services at several major U.S. banks experienced problems for several hours after an issue with JPMorgan Chase's systems. Today, CNN reported that a highly classified communications network used by the National Security Agency (NSA) went down.

articles.title_orig: New Nvidia boss says 'ambition has never been greater' after Jensen Huang's exit
articles.title_zh: New Nvidia boss says 'ambition has never been greater' after Jensen Huang's exit
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
This afternoon, Colette Kress gets the biggest microphone of her career.
The longtime Nvidia ( NVDA ) CFO — who is known to shun the spotlight her former boss craved — is now the company's interim CEO.
And she's about to face Wall Street for the first time without Jensen Huang — the founder, the face, and the architect of the extraordinary AI machine that has upended markets and the economy.
Talk about a pressure test!
Let me be blunt: Nvidia and Kress do not need to wax poetic on the earnings call about another good quarter. They need to convince nervous investors that the business can keep delivering extraordinary growth without the person who built it.
The bar to appeasing Wall Street right now is enormous. Investors want confidence in the next quarter, the next generation of chips, the customers spending hundreds of billions on AI infrastructure — and the leadership team running the show.
They also want to know how Kress plans to handle dealmaking differently than her former boss, who has loved handing out cash and promises to the AI ecosystem.
Kress has spent years explaining Nvidia's numbers to Wall Street and, in the process, has become one of the most respected CFOs in the game. Tonight, she has to explain Nvidia's future without someone wearing a black leather jacket at all events.
And that's a very different job.
Because the question hanging over this company isn't just whether AI demand is real.
It's whether Nvidia can remain Nvidia without Jensen Huang.
I think Kress is up to the task. She knows the company. She gets the moment. And I believe she will deliver a reminder of why she has been the CFO of rocketship Nvidia for more than 13 years.
I'll be back tonight with a special live Sozzi Unleashed right after Kress wraps her earnings call. That's where you'll want to be for instant analysis.

articles.title_orig: The Nvidia Scandal Is Only Half the Story of China’s AI Workarounds
articles.title_zh: The Nvidia Scandal Is Only Half the Story of China’s AI Workarounds
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Former Nvidia boss Jensen Huang has said he would be “honoured” to return to the company after he was ousted in the wake of a scandal.
Mr Huang resigned from the chipmaker last week, amid a wave of scandal after he admitted to an affair with a woman accused of being a Chinese spy as well as a subordinate at Nvidia . Since then, petitions and supporters have called for him to return – but the company has said that it is not interested in inviting him back.
Nonetheless, Mr Huang signalled he would be willing to return and that he would work with an investigation into the incident. But he suggested that the decision was up to the board and whether it thought his return would be “in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America”.
“Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said in his first public statement since he resigned on 12 November over revelations of extramarital affairs that intensified scrutiny of the chip firm's China business. Mr Huang had not been quoted in Nvidia’s original statement about his departure, though it thanked him for his “profound” contributions to the company, and he has been silent since.
“I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation,” he said in the new statement.
Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Mr Huang's statement, but multiple reports have suggested that its board is not planning to reappoint him. Nvidia shares ⁠pared some declines and were last down 1 per cent.
More than 180,000 people have signed a petition demanding Huang’s return, Elon Musk has thrown his support behind the effort, ⁠and US President Donald Trump said he would not mind seeing Huang reinstated as CEO. Thousands of people identifying themselves as Nvidia employees have joined the call, even as governance experts and some investors warn that bringing him back before investigations are complete could expose the company to fresh risks.
The groundswell of support for Huang has turned a corporate succession story into a test of whether Nvidia can separate itself from a founder whose influence stretches across its employees — some fiercely loyal to the former CEO — and shareholders, Silicon Valley, the Taiwanese supply chain and Washington.
Taiwan's tallest skyscraper, Taipei 101, was illuminated on Monday with messages including "Taiwan Loves Jensen." Some prominent shareholders such as Atreides ⁠Management's Gavin Baker and Altimeter Capital Management CEO Brad Gerstner have urged Nvidia not to rush to replace him ​before ⁠all the facts are known.
Earlier on Tuesday, before Mr Huang’s statement, Nvidia created a board-level ​committee ⁠to oversee national security and export controls, its first major governance move since he left.
Mr Huang's relationships have raised questions about whether Nvidia's oversight kept pace with its rapid growth and increasing importance to US national security. The crisis had erased more ⁠than $400 billion from the company's market value by Monday's close.
The National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee will be chaired by director Suzanne Nora Johnson, ​a former Goldman Sachs ⁠vice chair, Nvidia said. Directors Stephen Neal, former CEO of ‌law firm Cooley, and John Dabiri, a Caltech professor, will also serve on the committee.
Donald Trump welcomed the move, calling the launch of a national security initiative a good idea.
In the full statement, posted on X, Mr Huang thanked the public for its support and admitted to having made “serious mistakes”. He also included a message to his family, in which he suggested they were offering him “support”.
“Over the past week, I’ve been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I've never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me,” he wrote.
“I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen is one of the greatest gifts and proudest moments of my life. Nvidia has been my life’s work. Building it into the company it is today alongside my colleagues has been a privilege and an honor. Nowhere but in America could a company like Nvidia be possible. I love our country, and I love Nvidia.
“I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at Nvidia, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation.
“Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honoured to answer these calls and return as CEO.
“Thank you again to everyone who has shared their good wishes. I am profoundly humbled by your support. To my family: I love you, and I will spend the rest of my life being worthy of yours.”

articles.title_orig: UK hands NATO-assigned US soldier accused of Russia spying to US military
articles.title_zh: UK hands NATO-assigned US soldier accused of Russia spying to US military
articles.content_orig:
A senior United States soldier assigned to NATO who was arrested in Britain last week on suspicion of spying for Russia has been transferred to US military custody, United Kingdom police have said.
The Head of Counter Terrorism Police (CTP), Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, said on Tuesday that authorities in London have passed the investigation to US partners “in line with existing international protocols”.
The 41-year-old man was arrested by British police on November 10 near Gloucester on suspicion of offences under Section 1 and Section 3 of the UK National Security Act 2023.
Section 1 relates to obtaining or disclosing protected information, while Section 3 relates to assisting a foreign intelligence service.
“These are extremely serious allegations, and our collective response should send a strong message that we will act swiftly and robustly where we suspect this kind of espionage activity taking place,” Taylor said.
He added, “We will continue to support our US colleagues as they take the matter forwards.”
US FBI Director Kash Patel said the army officer is in US custody as a “result of an espionage investigation” between the FBI’s Philadelphia field office and Legat London in addition to partners at “UK Counter Terrorism Policing, MI5, UK Defence Counter Intelligence, and the US Army Counterintelligence Command.”
Brigadier General Sean Stinchon, the commanding general of US Army Counterintelligence Command (ACIC), said the case illustrated the “remarkable partnership” between ACIC, US Army prosecutors, the FBI, the US Department of Justice, and the UK.
Stinchon added that this example sends a “stark warning to any service member suspected of violating the oath”.
The case is believed to be the first time a US soldier was found to be under suspicion of spying for a foreign government while in the UK.

articles.title_orig: Putin's Crimean Bridge partly collapses as Zelensky hails 'unprecedented' attack by Ukraine
articles.title_zh: Putin's Crimean Bridge partly collapses as Zelensky hails 'unprecedented' attack by Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
Ukraine has severely damaged a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, in what President Volodymyr Zelensky says was an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making.
Images shared by Ukrainian officials show a section of the Crimean Bridge collapsed into the water, dealing a logistical and symbolic blow to Moscow's war effort.
The Kremlin said it would rebuild the bridge "better than before".
Meanwhile in Kyiv, Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko said traffic had partially resumed on the Pivnichnyi (Northern) and Pivdennyi (Southern) bridges - key crossings over the Dnipro River - after they had been closed following Russian strikes overnight.
Ukraine has long targeted the Crimean Bridge, which provides a road and rail route for Russian soldiers heading towards the front line, but has struggled to close it for good.
While Kyiv has been trying to increase the cost to Russia of waging war economically, by hitting oil refineries and depots, striking the bridge is an attempt to increase the political cost on Russian President Vladimir Putin.
The timing of the strike comes at a significant moment, ahead of Putin meeting the leaders of China and the US. This could cloud his moment back in the spotlight.
The Crimean Bridge was built by Russia after it invaded and illegally annexed Ukraine's southern peninsula in 2014.
The $3.6bn (£2.7bn) piece of infrastructure is widely seen in Russia and Ukraine as Putin's personal pet project: His close tycoon friend Arkady Rotenberg built it, and then Putin personally opened it by driving a lorry over it in May 2018.
In Ukraine, the much-hated bridge is seen as one of the main symbols of Russia's continuing occupation of Ukrainian lands.
"We're drinking champagne!" Andrii, an engineer who lives in Kyiv, told the BBC.
He said the latest attack would "deal a very heavy blow to the morale of the Russians".
Some Ukrainians are concerned that Putin might now respond by carrying out even more attacks against civilian infrastructure, but Andrii said: "I don't think the Russians can make things much worse; they're already pounding us every single night with everything they've got."
The damage after the overnight attack, involving cruise missiles and drones, appeared to be far more severe than during previous strikes on the bridge, with a large arched section apparently destroyed.
Video footage appeared to show critical damage to the road section, with remnants of the support arch and road deck seen protruding from the water below.
Zelensky said the strike was the result of a seven-stage operation by the military and security services, which saw Ukrainian forces "gradually destroy air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare equipment, and other designated targets on the way to the final objective".
He said several types of Ukrainian drones as well as the country's Flamingo and Neptune cruise missiles were fired overnight during a "pivotal stage".
The Ukrainian president also said the rail section parallel to the bridge's road had also been hit by a wave of drones, though images showed its supporting arch was still standing and Russia's transport ministry later said some rail services resumed.
Ukraine's state security service SBU said its operations had "systematically suppressed enemy air defence systems" over a month, and said it showed "no Russian defence systems can guarantee the safety of illegal objects occupied by the invaders".
Meanwhile, Ukraine's military said the roadway on the bridge is "out of action", with no vehicle able to cross it, and the railway section is still standing, but with a damaged arch.
The Kremlin said Putin had been briefed on the overnight attack. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the bridge would "be restored following Ukrainian strikes, and it will be even better than before", and did not rule out the possibility the strikes were linked to Putin's visit to China.
Russia's Investigative Committee confirmed structural damage and said it had opened a "criminal case... on terrorism charges" after attacks by "Ukraine's armed formations".
For the second day in a row, Russia recorded the biggest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began, with 2,256 drones downed, according to the defence ministry.
Zelensky had warned of major attacks in the days leading up to a meeting between Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in China's Shenzhen on Thursday.
In Kyiv, loud explosions were heard just before midnight on Monday, with Klitschko saying shortly after that the city had suffered "damage to critical infrastructure systems" and disruption to heating and water supplies.
On Tuesday, Zelensky said four ballistic missiles had targeted the Southern Bridge, and another three had been fired on the Northern Bridge.
Some of Kyiv's above-ground metro services were also damaged in the overnight attacks, local officials said, after civilians were told to go to civil defence shelters.
Eight major bridges span the Dnipro River, connecting the western and eastern parts of Kyiv, and an estimated three million residents rely on the bridges to travel across the city.
Elsewhere, three people have been injured in a Russian missile attack in the central Cherkasy region, according to local officials.
The long-term impact of the Crimean Bridge strike is still not fully clear, though the risk of a serious transport and logistics crisis for the Russian military has increased significantly.
The collapse of the arched section has cut off the peninsula's direct road and rail links with Russia – at least until the crossing can be repaired.
However, there is still a land corridor running through the occupied parts of Ukraine's southern Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions - though Kyiv has been systematically striking transport routes across northern Crimea, as well as bridges and other crossings in the area around Chongar.
This has already caused problems with the delivery of fuel and other supplies, including military cargo.
There is a ferry crossing across the Kerch Strait, which connects the Black Sea with the Sea of Azov. It could partly compensate for the loss of the bridge, but its capacity is very limited and it is also vulnerable to attack.
Russia could also supply Crimea by sea, but this route is also risky, as Ukrainian naval and aerial drones operate extensively in the area.
In addition, debris from the Crimean Bridge – particularly its enormous arch – may have blocked the shipping channel.
This would make it harder for larger vessels to pass through and create further problems for the Russian-occupied ports in the Sea of Azov, including Mariupol and Berdyansk.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Approximately one-fifth of Ukraine is now under Russian occupation and Kyiv has refused Putin's demand to give up areas of Ukraine's eastern Donbas that remain under its control.
Additional reporting by Jaroslav Lukiv

articles.title_orig: ‘Do not build’: UK sanctions 8 Israeli construction companies for building West Bank settlements
articles.title_zh: ‘Do not build’: UK sanctions 8 Israeli construction companies for building West Bank settlements
articles.content_orig:
The UK has sanctioned companies it said are involved in building settlements in the occupied West Bank, in the first package of measures since the government announced a tougher approach to Israeli actions in the territory.
The government said the sanctions against eight construction and property development firms would disrupt their flows of finance and ability to support building in the West Bank.
The construction of settlements, which are illegal under international law, has risen sharply in recent years. Settler attacks on Palestinians and their property have also surged.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar called the sanctions a "hostile act targeting private, law-abiding companies".
Criticising the move on X, he wrote that Israel - as it has done in the past - will respond with "countermeasures", and that "decisions will be announced in due course".
"Israel will not bow to external pressure or change its policies as a result," Saar said, adding that they will "consider new ways to strengthen Jewish communities" in the West Bank, and "protect those involved in developing and building".
Israel previously condemned UK sanctions related to West Bank settlements, accusing the Labour government of "systematically acting against the State of Israel".
The Palestinian foreign ministry welcomed the sanctions and called on other countries to follow suit.
It comes two days before the deadline for bids for construction tenders in the highly sensitive E1 area east of Jerusalem.
The plans, which have been condemned internationally, would in effect divide the West Bank in two and cut it off from East Jerusalem.
UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has said the E1 development would render a two-state solution "unviable" by "cutting through the heart of Palestine".
The sanctions also target Tzav 9, an Israeli activist movement which the UK government says has organised and carried out blockades to prevent aid entering Gaza.
Responding to the announcement, the group said: "Tzav 9 is a movement of abiding citizens from all the political spectrum, and we've always protested peacefully."
It comes after the UK expanded its human rights sanctions regime last month, enabling the government to sanction individuals and companies involved in violations of international humanitarian law anywhere in the world.
The government is also developing separate legislation to ban the import of goods from Israeli settlements and the provision of advertising services for settlement properties in the UK.
Miliband said: "Protecting the two-state solution is the North Star of this government's approach.
"That is why my message on E1 is clear: do not bid, do not build, and do not profit from the destruction of the two-state solution.
"The status quo in the West Bank and Gaza is unacceptable.
"We are committed to working productively with a new Israeli government and the Palestinian Authority to advance lasting peace and security for Israelis and Palestinians alike."
In September, the UK government announced that it would ban the import of goods from Israeli settlements, as well as acting against companies and individuals providing services for settlement expansion.
At the time, Miliband said the move marked the beginning of a "new approach" to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, which "not only calls out injustice and suffering, but acts".
That announcement prompted a furious reaction from Israel , which said it would shut the British consulate in East Jerusalem in retaliation.
Last month, most diplomats left the consulate - which handled UK relations with Palestinians in Jerusalem as well as in the West Bank and Gaza - but the UK insisted that the building would not be closing and would operate as a "UK mission".
Israel has built about 160 settlements housing 700,000 Jews since it occupied the West Bank and East Jerusalem during the 1967 Middle East war. An estimated 3.3 million Palestinians live alongside them.
There has been a surge in attacks by settlers on Palestinians and their property in the West Bank since the start of the Gaza war, which was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023.

articles.title_orig: Following Microsoft Outlook, Teams, Gmail outage has hit. Marriott down too [Update]
articles.title_zh: Following Microsoft Outlook, Teams, Gmail outage has hit. Marriott down too [Update]
articles.content_orig:
Was Google feeling a little left out of the recent wave of tech outages? The company took to X on Tuesday to announce that its Gmail service is actually running just fine. In a post, the company said it was not currently seeing evidence of a broad Gmail service disruption and reminded users they could always check Gmail’s real-time status on its online dashboard .
As it turns out, the company was trying to head off reports of a Gmail outage that began circulating on X on Tuesday around the same time that Apple was seeing a number of verified outages of its own . While some posts on the social network suggested Gmail was experiencing a disruption, others said they were not having any problems.
The concerns seemed to stem from an X post by Downdetector, a crowdsourced website where users can report service disruptions themselves and see if others are having problems. Downdetector is not an official source for verifying or understanding the true scope of internet outages, and as people become more concerned about possible cyberattacks, the site’s data may become less valuable over time if every minor glitch and hiccup is reported as an “outage” by non-technical users.
The fact that Google had to announce it was not having an outage speaks to the growing anxiety around the reliability of major tech services. Over the past week, Apple and Microsoft experienced outages, an FAA network failure led to a nationwide ground stop, and some banks and airlines also reported disruptions.
However, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said on Fox Business Network’s “The Claman Countdown” on Tuesday that the U.S. is not currently facing coordinated cyberattacks. He told the outlet, “We do not see the indicia of a coordinated cyberattack — let me just be clear about that — and we do not see the indicia of state-sponsored activity here.”
Instead, Clayton attributed the rise in issues to businesses patching their systems. The patching may be a downstream effect of AI, as newer models have become increasingly adept at uncovering previously unknown vulnerabilities. “They’re upgrading them, they’re putting patches in place,” he said, adding that this is happening at “a much larger scale” than before.
As a result, some of the systems are “not coming back as expected in all cases,” he added.

articles.content_orig:
Nvidia warned its customers that new legislation on Chinese companies remotely accessing its artificial-intelligence chips could expose it and them to U.S. "legal action," sources told CNBC.
The chip giant is facing increasing scrutiny from U.S. lawmakers over Chinese companies' access to its advanced chips, which U.S. export controls restrict from going to China.
Nvidia messaged chip buyers in recent months to caution that the proposed Remote Access Security Act, or RASA, would give the U.S. government broader authority to control access to cloud services in the same way as physical hardware, potentially exposing both parties to legal risk, according to two people with direct knowledge of the matter. The people asked not to be named while discussing private communications.
It also said that, for now, it would not sell its chips to customers who rent more than 50% of the graphics processing units, or GPUs, to Chinese companies, the people said.
Separately, the Financial Times reported earlier this month that Nvidia verbally told data-center clients to direct at least 51% of their services to non-Chinese customers under future contracts.
Regulators have had limited powers to control companies' access to those chips through cloud services hosted overseas.
RASA passed the House of Representatives in January but has not yet passed the Senate. Remote access to the chips has provoked the ire of President Donald Trump 's administration, which has sought to keep the chips out of China to maintain the U.S. lead in the AI race.
CNBC reported on Nov. 5 that Chinese lab Moonshot AI sought access to Nvidia chips through data centers in Europe. The Trump administration previously singled the company out, accusing it in July of accessing the chips through centers in East Asia.
The U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, announced on Monday an interim final rule designed to prevent Chinese companies' remote access to AI chips.
Nvidia and BIS did not respond to a request for comment.
On Sunday, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called for a "dramatic shakeup" at Nvidia after Jensen Huang 's shock departure as CEO, amid reports of an extramarital affair with a woman U.S. authorities reportedly suspect of spying for China.
Bessent suggested other Nvidia executives should face scrutiny over the chip giant's compliance with export controls.
"I want to keep coming back to what was the culture at Nvidia, and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?" Bessent told Fox News.
In an August securities filing , Nvidia said it sought to "strictly comply with all applicable export control regulators" but did not have "physical control of our products after sale" and relied on its customers' and partners' compliance programs.
Huang has been asked to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 3.

articles.title_orig: Wall Street ends lower ahead of Nvidia earnings, Anthropic debut
articles.title_zh: Wall Street ends lower ahead of Nvidia earnings, Anthropic debut
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia shares closed marginally lower Tuesday as former CEO Jensen Huang released his first public statement since his resignation and the company prepares to report earnings after the bell.
The stock move Tuesday marked Nvidia's fourth straight daily decline.
In the statement, Huang said he is open to returning as Nvidia's CEO and that he is committed to cooperating with the board's investigation into his behavior.
"I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret," Huang said in a statement obtained by CNBC's David Faber . "I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board's independent investigation."
"If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO," Huang continued.
Huang resigned from Nvidia, the company's board announced on Thursday, following reports that he had a relationship with a woman U.S. intelligence reportedly believes to be a Chinese spy. Huang told employees he had an affair in an email on Nov. 8. Outlets also reported that Huang also had an affair with a vice president at the company and an "intimate relationship" with an unnamed second employee.
Nvidia's stock slid 4% on Monday, bringing shares to their lowest close since July 1, 2025.
Lawmakers also announced Tuesday that Huang will appear before the House Foreign Affairs, Intelligence, and China Select Committees on Dec. 1. Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter will appear before the same committees on Dec. 2.
Nvidia's stock slid 4% on Monday, bringing shares to their lowest close since July 1, 2025.
An online petition calling for Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO drew more than 190,000 signatures , including Elon Musk . But Nvidia's board of directors is not considering bringing back Jensen Huang as CEO, a person familiar with the matter told CNBC on Monday.
The chip giant is also facing increasing scrutiny from U.S. lawmakers over Chinese companies' access to its advanced chips, which U.S. export controls restrict from going to China.
The U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, announced on Monday an interim final rule designed to prevent Chinese companies' remote access to AI chips.
Nvidia announced on Tuesday morning that its board had established a committee responsible for oversight of the company's national security policies, export control compliance and global trade risk management.
The National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee will be chaired by director Suzanne Nora Johnson and will include directors Stephen C. Neal and John O. Dabiri as members, the company said in a statement.

articles.title_orig: Facing Criticism, Trump Administration Says It’s Investigating Megaspeed
articles.title_zh: Facing Criticism, Trump Administration Says It’s Investigating Megaspeed
articles.content_orig:
The United States has confirmed it is investigating computing company Megaspeed, suspecting it of violating US export controls by helping to ship tech giant Nvidia's chips to China.
In a joint statement, the US Department of Justice and Department of Commerce said they had been investigating Singapore-based firm Megaspeed since 2024.
It comes after questions were raised about the possibility high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.
Concerns emerged in recent weeks after Nvidia founder Jensen Huang revealed he had an extramarital affair , allegedly with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang. US authorities suspect her of spying for Beijing, which China denies.
Jensen Huang resigned from his role as chief executive last week following revelations he had two affairs.
Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in South East Asia and is suspected of helping divert advanced chips to China. The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business.
The justice and commerce departments said on Monday that "it is in the public interest to provide the facts and address inaccurate information" regarding the investigation.
Laying out a timeline, it said it began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 "for potential export control violations".
In May 2025, Department of Commerce investigators requested records from Nvidia "concerning direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed". In June 2025, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its 'no sell' list.
Agents from the Bureau of Industry and Security, in conjunction with Singaporean law enforcement officials, then conducted an on-site check at Megaspeed that month and interviewed Alice Huang, who was chief executive at the time.
Following this enforcement action, the Department of Justice took the lead role in the criminal investigation of Megaspeed.
The Nvidia scandal has created tensions between the US Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end chips to Megaspeed.
On Friday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed the US Commerce Department, led by Howard Lutnick, for failing to properly oversee the export of the chips.
Lutnick has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over his department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.
While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.
Huang has agreed to testify in Congress, including before the House Select Committee on China to discuss whether US national security was compromised by his affair.
The White House said on Monday it would further restrict China's access to AI chips from firms like Nvidia.
The reported affairs by Jensen Huang created a crisis for one of the world's most valuable firms - a major company in the AI industry and central to the US as it competes with China for dominance.
In the statement, the US government said it would "bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred".
They added: "Sensitive technologies like semiconductors are among the most valuable and strategic assets of the US economy, and the Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce will remain vigilant in pursuing justice for those who want to compromise America's technological edge."

articles.title_orig: Ukraine Talks Run Up Against Deep Enmity Between Russia and Europe
articles.title_zh: Ukraine Talks Run Up Against Deep Enmity Between Russia and Europe
articles.content_orig:
But the Europeans should lead the process of changing it.
After an eight-month pause, trilateral talks aimed at ending the Russia–Ukraine War resumed in Abu Dhabi last week , this time with an updated focus: Europe’s security architecture. In the lead up to the meeting, President Donald Trump’s envoy and son-in-law, Jared Kushner, described the goal : “to develop practical arrangements that address the security concerns of all sides, reduce the risk of future conflict, and create a more stable and predictable security environment.”
European leaders immediately and loudly objected to this new direction , with some calling it a clear concession to the Kremlin. But this reaction is misplaced. Any discussion over how to end the war must address the shape of Europe’s security order for the simple reason that it is the flaws, shortcomings, and inconsistencies of the existing system that led to the outbreak of the conflict in the first place.
Washington should not, however, underestimate the challenges involved in updating Europe’s security arrangements. A lasting solution will require not just European buy-in, but European leadership and the development of rules capable of managing what will be a contested and adversarial relationship between Russia and its neighbors for many years to come.
Opponents of this broader focus have put forward a litany of reasons why the question of security architecture should be excluded from negotiations, at least at this stage.
For some, the complaint is one of sequencing. They argue the discussions about modifying Europe’s security system can only begin once the fighting in Ukraine stops . History, however, suggests that this is unrealistic. Negotiations to end long-running bitter conflicts almost always occur as fighting continues on the battlefield. Talks to end the Korean War , for instance, started in 1951, about a year after the war began, but no deal was reached until 1953, after over 150 rounds of negotiations.
For other critics, the concern is not one of timing, but the simple fact that Europe’s security architecture is on the table at all. Europe already has a security architecture , they argue, and it is based around the EU and NATO. If it needs updating (and some believe it does not), it is no business of Moscow’s. After all, they assert, Russia has repeatedly violated its commitments and shouldn’t get a say in Europe’s security in any case.
There are several problems with this position, however. First, Paris Charter , signed in 1990 to govern post–Cold War relations between Russia and the rest of Europe, is 36 years old and badly out of date, built to manage a Europe that looked very different than what exists today. Since then, the Soviet Union dissolved, NATO expanded to include 32 members, the European Economic Community became the European Union , and that organization took in new members. Yugoslavia broke into independent states after a series of brutal civil wars in which NATO interfered. Wars have been fought in Georgia and Ukraine, and most arms control treaties between the U.S., NATO, and Russia have expired. The balance of economic and military power on the continent has shifted. That a system set up for a fundamentally different Europe is not up to the task of managing today’s security relationships should not be controversial.
Second, to define Europe’s security architecture as sufficiently robust because it has NATO and the EU is a strange distortion. If true, then Europe’s security order excludes the dozen or so European countries that are not members of either organization (for instance, both Russia and Ukraine) but incorporates Canada and the United States which lie an ocean away. Surely Russia deserves more of a say in Europe’s security architecture, of which it must be a part, than does the United States.
And finally, it is not only Moscow that has shown an interest in revising the security architecture established in Europe at the end of the Cold War. The United States and both NATO and the EU have made their own changes to the rules and shape of Europe’s security order since 1990, often violating the spirit of agreements signed at the time. Their most recent updates occurred less than five years ago, when Finland and Sweden joined NATO. Although NATO’s eastward expansion is not technically prohibited by past agreements, the encroachment of its forces and military infrastructure toward the Russian border has clearly violated the Paris Charter’s commitment to “indivisible security” by making new NATO members more secure at Russia’s expense.
From Moscow’s perspective, then, a request to revisit Europe’s security architecture is justified on at least two grounds: first, that this security order has been altered numerous times over the past four decades, sometimes by Russia but more often by NATO and EU members; and second, that Russia too is a member of Europe and deserves a say in the “European security order.”
It is not a concession to Russia, but to reality, to acknowledge that shortcomings of Europe’s post-Cold War security architecture, including disagreements about who is included and who is not, are among the most important causes of the war in Ukraine . Russia’s primary objection has been the gradual development of a European security system that encompasses its neighbors while leaving Russia itself on the outside. This does not justify Russia’s use of force, but it does suggest that any lasting resolution to the conflict in Ukraine will require steps toward an updated security arrangement that formally incorporates the changes that have occurred over the past three decades, clarifies questions of membership, and addresses the grievances of Russia and its European neighbors in an enduring way.
The U.S. is therefore right to bring this issue into ongoing trilateral talks now. Addressing the so-called “root causes” of the conflict is indeed a Russian demand, but it is also in Ukraine’s and Europe’s interests if the aim is a stable peace that guards against the recurrence of war. The question, then, is not whether Europe’s security order should be incorporated into ongoing talks but rather how to address this issue, given its complexity.
So far, the U.S. approach has been ineffective. By seeming ready to work with Moscow over the heads of the Europeans, U.S. negotiators have exacerbated Europe’s perception of insecurity without achieving any real progress. It is clear that Washington cannot “deliver Europe” as some in Russia might have hoped when Trump returned to the White House in 2025.
A better strategy would be to have Europe lead the renegotiation of its security architecture directly, with the U.S. acting not as mediator, but as supporting player. The Trump administration has already indicated that it expects Europe to manage its own conventional deterrence and take on more responsibility for its own defense. Since they are the ones who will have to implement any new security system and carry its burdens increasingly without U.S. involvement, it should also be up to Europe’s leaders to define how that future system will be organized and how it will incorporate Russia.
To this point, much of Europe has not been ready to talk seriously with Russia about the continent’s security order. This is changing due to Europe’s fear that it will be left out of discussions likely to affect its future and its understanding that the price of a seat at the table in ongoing negotiations over the Russia–Ukraine War is a willingness to engage with Moscow.
However, Europe’s readiness to talk is just a first step. A dialogue to devise a new European security architecture will not be quick or easy and it is unrealistic to think that it will be complete soon. The EU and Russia have both put forward maximalist proposals and negotiating from these to a mutually acceptable outcome will be challenging. articles.title_orig: Senate Democrats demand briefings about FAA ground stop amid $50B budget ask - ABC News
articles.title_zh: Senate Democrats demand briefings about FAA ground stop amid $50B budget ask - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
The funding would go to new air traffic control centers and other improvements.
Democrats on the Senate Commerce Committee sent a letter to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Federal Aviation Administration's Bryan Bedford on Tuesday demanding an explanation for Friday's nationwide ground stop and calling for briefings before there are additional changes to the air traffic control system.
It comes the same day the Department of Transportation has officially submitted its $50.1 billion budget funding request -- a marked increase -- to fix a system Duffy and President Donald Trump say is broken . The budget breakdown includes more than $10 billion for the completion of a reliable digital architecture, more than $10 billion to overhaul outdated airport infrastructure, $10 billion to build five new air traffic control centers and another $10 billion to build and improve up to 140 air traffic control towers.
Duffy has said the $50 billion funding ask, which is in addition to the $12.5 billion that was appropriated by Congress, is needed to fix the issues that led to the ground stop.
"This is an emergency," he told reporters Friday night. "I want Congress to give us emergency funding. This is bipartisan. This is American. I want $50 billion."
In their letter, Democrats said that Friday's ground stop "disrupted air travel across the country, eroded public trust in our aviation system, and raised serious questions" about the FAA and its ability to ensure reliable operations.
"Congress expects clear, fact-based answers about the root cause of this disruption and why existing safeguards failed to prevent it," the 13 Democrats on the committee wrote in the letter.
The senators addressed Duffy's funding request -- noting that the increase from $30 billion to $50 billion following Friday's ground stop "is notably $20 billion more than the request from DOT and the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) that was sent on Thursday, November 12."
"DOT, FAA and OMB must provide Congress with a complete account of what happened and how additional funding would address the vulnerabilities presented on November 13," the senators wrote.
Ahead of a meeting with Duffy on Tuesday, Republican Sen. Thom Tillis said the funding request needs to be detailed.
"If you want $30 billion or $50 billion, you better damn sure have a long list of initiatives and planning that went into it versus ‘give me a number and I'll figure out how to spend it.’”
GOP Sen. John Cornyn said when it comes to FAA funding, he would like to know "what they have, why they haven't spent it and why they need more."
The Democratic senators also raised questions about devices from Juniper -- the company that manufactured the routers believed to be central to the ground stop -- as well as L3 Harris, a government contractor that provides technology and IT support for the FAA and that worked with Hewlett Packard Enterprise and Juniper to install the routers.
The ground stop happened because of a telecommunications issue, both Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said on Friday; FAA Administrator Bedford added that it was the result of faulty equipment.
Duffy told ABC's "This Week" Sunday that work was being done to replace outdated copper wire with fiber cables in El Dorado, Arkansas, when the router communication believed to have caused the ground stop occurred. When the router in that area was turned on, "we saw that in Amarillo, Texas, a system we had replaced about three weeks earlier, that started to flood our system as well," Duffy explained.
In the letter, the senators requested a pause on the installation of additional Juniper devices -- the devices that are replacing routers in the copper-to-fiber transition -- until further testing demonstrates that they can be deployed safely.
The lawmakers say they expect a briefing on those improvements before installation continues.
"Deployment should resume after the FAA demonstrates the devices' readiness for safe deployment through improved operational testing, independent validation, verified failover capability, and rollback procedures," they said.
The FAA announced Tuesday afternoon that it was halting the installation of Juniper routers .
The senators requested technical briefings from the FAA, L3 Harris and Juniper by Monday. Those briefings should include an initial safety assessment and explanations about how the system lacked sufficient redundancy to immediately recover during Friday's ground stop, the senators wrote in the letter.
The outage, they write, has left them "concerned" about DOT's ability to oversee the new air traffic control system.
"Modernization cannot come at the expense of operational safety," they wrote.
Asked for comment on the letter, a DOT spokesperson said "The Department has provided updates as we have them and will continue to do so."
Sen. Tammy Duckworth, the ranking member of the Commerce Aviation, Space and Innovation subcommittee who is among the Democrats who signed the letter, has said Duffy is "unfit to serve" in his role if he is not able to answer questions about the ground stop.
"If the Secretary cannot take responsibility and provide answers, he is unfit to serve as the Secretary of Transportation," Duckworth said in a statement to Politico.
Trump has praised Duffy amid concern over the ground stop, saying on Monday that Duffy is "doing a great job."
ABC News' Lalee Ibssa contributed to this report.

Taiwan is likely to be overshadowed as presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump are expected to meet on the sidelines of the Asia Pacific Economic Forum this week, even as the threat from China evolves and grows stronger.
Leaders from China, the U.S. and some 21 other economies will gather at the APEC summit this week in Shenzhen, China. Recent events like the scandal that forced Nvidia's CEO to resign, export controls and the ongoing trade dispute have made the tech competition between Beijing and Washington all the more pressing.
Few expect major breakthroughs on Taiwan, a self-ruled island that is claimed by Beijing. While the U.S. does not formally recognize Taiwan, it is the island’s biggest informal ally and seller of arms.
“For the Trump administration, this isn’t a core issue between the U.S. and China,” said Arthur Zhin-Sheng Wang, an expert on cross-Straits relations at Taiwan’s Central Police University.
US-Taiwan ties remain strong behind the scenes
Experts largely say that cooperation with the U.S. remains strong below the level of rhetoric, despite Trump’s public ambivalence toward Taiwan.
One sign of this came from the summer, when the de facto United States embassy in Taiwan posted a photo showing joint patrols between the two coast guards, a rare occurrence, as the U.S. does not usually acknowledge it has direct cooperation with Taiwan in any defense capacity.
“This also is proof of the decades that Taiwan and U.S. have had of cooperation and training. I was also surprised,” said Kuo Yu-jen, a defense studies expert and director of the Institute for National Policy Research in Taiwan.
The U.S. is obligated by law to help Taiwan defend itself, which has manifested in the form of arms sales, while the government officially adopts a stance of ambiguity on whether it would intervene militarily in the case of a Chinese invasion.
The Taiwanese public is used to the continued uncertainties of the island’s relationship with the U.S. Research from the Institute of National Defense and Security Research in Taiwan, a government-funded think tank, showed that public attitudes toward the U.S. remain around the same. Polls conducted in the past five years show that about half of the public believes the U.S. will send soldiers to support Taiwan in the event of a Chinese invasion, and about half don’t.
“I do think they will take some actions, though it may not be sending soldiers,” said Allen Hsieh, a 28-year-old media professional in Taipei. “I think Taiwan’s importance to the U.S. is even more important than Ukraine.”
Stalled arms sales for now
Since starting his second term, Trump called for Taiwan to spend more on its own defense and Taiwan responded that it would commit to 5% of its GDP on defense.
Arms sales are ongoing. While much media attention has focused on a $14 billion package that remains stalled, an earlier package of $11 billion approved at the end of last year is in progress. Some of the stalled arms packages have been delayed since before Trump came into office, experts have also said.
Those include fighter jets. Taiwan received the first two of long-delayed F-16V fighter jets from the U.S. in October, and three more jets earlier this month. The aircraft are a part of a long list of backlogged U.S. orders worth almost $30 billion, according to the Taiwan Security Monitor research project which tracks defense-related developments on the island at George Mason University.
But the delays are not necessarily because of political considerations with China, a concern that was raised when Trump said he discussed arms sales with Xi earlier this year. Instead, it may be more of an issue with manufacturing capacity, particularly for future sales.
Congress approved the sale of long-range precision strike systems to Taiwan in December 2025, but Taiwan faces competition because of limited supplies. Kuo noted that among the missiles approved for sale are the same ones being used by the U.S. military in the ongoing Iran war, such as the HIMARS rockets and supplies were low.
“I don’t think this is a political issue. They just can’t produce so many of these missiles in a short period,” he said.
China expands coast guard role in pressure on Taiwan
Meanwhile, China has intensified its military and nonmilitary pressure on Taiwan. In 2025, the People’s Liberation Army flew about 5,448 fighter jet sorties toward the island during military exercises, according to Skyfaring, an open-source website that compiles public data from Taiwan’s Ministry of Defense. That marked a sharp increase from the years before 2023, when such flights were sporadic.
Beijing also recently held unannounced military drills in the Western Pacific, deploying more than 100 vessels in waters near Taiwan and Japan, Taiwan’s National Security Council chief Joseph Wu said in a Nov. 3 post on X.
The number of PLA flights recorded this year stood at 2,401 as of Nov. 12, below the full-year total for 2025.
“I think the threat is transforming ... for example, more of its exercises are now about blockading and sealing off” Taiwan, Wang said, rather than firing live missiles. He said Beijing was expanding its gray-zone tactics — aggressive actions that fall short of open warfare.
These include greater use of the coast guard to assert China’s claims, mirroring its approach elsewhere. In June, the Chinese coast guard began patrolling off Taiwan’s east coast, which faces the open Pacific, extending its activities beyond Taiwan’s outlying islands closer to China.
Wang compared the approach to Beijing’s tactics in the South China Sea, where Chinese coast guard vessels patrol waters disputed with the Philippines. China has also designated a shoal claimed by the Philippines as a nature reserve under Chinese protection.
“It’s telling the whole world it has sovereignty here.”

articles.title_orig: Memo to Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress: Remind the world why you've been Jensen Huang's CFO for 13-plus years
articles.title_zh: Memo to Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress: Remind the world why you've been Jensen Huang's CFO for 13-plus years
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia's quarterly sales doubled to top $100bn for the first time as the company insisted it has no plans to reinstate ousted co-founder Jensen Huang.
In the company's first results since Huang's dramatic exit , interim chief executive Colette Kress said it is "business as usual" and told investors: "We've got this."
The company's quarterly sales doubled from a year earlier, reaching $115.8bn (£86.9bn), with shares in the company jumping by 4.8% in after-hours trading.
Earlier on Tuesday, Huang said he would be "honoured" to return and lead Nvidia, having quit following alleged extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected spy for China.
"The board does not intend to reinstate him," Nvidia chair Harvey Jones said during a call on Tuesday with financial analysts.
The company's profits also doubled from a year ago. For the quarter, which covered the three months to 25 October, profit hit $65bn. Its revenue from data centres, a significant part of Nvidia's business, also doubled to $107bn in the same period.
Going forward, the company said its rapid growth is poised to continue, and revenue will rise by another 13% in the next quarter.
Given the uncertainty surrounding the company after Huang's exit, financial analysts had been unsure that Nvidia would provide any forward-looking guidance.
Daniela Hathorn, a senior analyst for trading platform Capital.com, said Nvidia's results "offer a strong answer to concerns that demand for AI infrastructure is cooling" and temper immediate worries that Huang was irreplaceable as a leader.
"The harder question is whether Nvidia can preserve the strategic advantage Huang helped build," Hathorn added. "His exit is unlikely to change orders already committed, but could matter more when Nvidia makes its next round of decisions on products, partnerships and investment."
Kress seemed eager to stress that Nvidia can continue to not only succeed, but lead the ongoing AI buildout that is happening throughout the technology industry.
"It is business as usual," she said. "Our partners, our suppliers, all of them are 100% behind us."
She added that Nvidia's leadership team has "stood up very strongly over the last week... working seamlessly in all of their departments and projects".
"Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed." Kress said before leaving the analyst call. "We've got this."
The interim CEO also said Nvidia is no longer shipping Hopper data centre semiconductors to China.
The Hopper technology is in Nvidia's advanced H200 processors, which the firm won approval to sell in China after Huang's repeated lobbying efforts in Washington.
They had previously been restricted over concerns that selling them to China would give its industries and military an edge over the US.
Kress did not elaborate on why the shipments had been stopped.
Despite board chairman Jones saying earlier that the company would not answer analysts' questions about Huang or Nvidia's investigation into his conduct, he did address the search for a permanent replacement.
He said Nvidia is working with an executive search firm and is considering internal and external candidates, but that the company would not rush its selection.
"With the advanced technology and the national security dynamics in the marketplace, our new CEO will have to navigate those waters carefully," Jones said. "The search will be thorough and we want to do it as quickly as possible, but we won't do it before we find the exact right person."
Michael Monaghan from investment firm Founder ETFs is among those who want Huang back in the top job at Nvidia.
The Nvidia investor told the BBC that he is waiting to see the results of a thorough investigation into Huang's actions, instead of relying on "salacious allegations" made in the media.
Nvidia's strong earnings are "from the machine that Jensen built" and a company tends to lose "its shine and vision" after an iconic founder leaves, Monaghan said.

articles.title_zh: The Game Awards 2026 Nominees – Play Gears of War: E-Day, Grand Theft Auto VI, Resident Evil Requiem, and More on XBOX
articles.content_orig:
By SHIVALI BEST, SCIENCE & TECHNOLOGY EDITOR
Published: 04:49 EST, 17 November 2026 | Updated: 04:49 EST, 17 November 2026
It's one of the most eagerly anticipated video games of all time.
Now, with just two days to go before Grand Theft Auto VI finally drops, experts have revealed the impact this could have on Britain's economy.
Research from Opinium suggests that a staggering 4.1 million working days could be lost across Britain, as avid gamers pull sick days and bunk off work.
'Few game launches generate the level of excitement we're seeing for GTA VI,' said James Nicandrou, Associate Director at Opinium.
'With huge numbers of gamers planning to take time off work, pull sick days or play while working from home, our research indicates the launch will have an impact well beyond the gaming world.
'The scale of expectation surrounding the game is striking. Not only do millions of Brits plan to buy it, but many already believe it could be one of the greatest games ever made.
'After more than a decade of waiting, expectations are running high.'
It's one of the most eagerly anticipated video games of all time. Now, with just two days to go before Grand Theft Auto VI finally drops, experts have revealed the impact this could have on Britain's economy
GTA VI is the latest entry in the franchise and is set to arrive on November 19, more than 13 years after GTA V, the second best-selling video game in history.
Ahead of its release, Opinium surveyed 2,000 Brits to find out their plans surrounding the game.
The results revealed that one in ten Brits who are planning to buy GTA VI will take a sick day to do so.
Another 12 per cent will play it while they're supposed to be working from home, while 15 per cent have proactively booked annual leave to get a proper gaming session in.
Those who are taking time off – whether it's as annual leave or as a sick day – say they'll need to take two days.
That equates to 4.1 million lost working days, according to Opinium.
Several eager gamers have taken to X to discuss their plans.
'I booked the 19th and 20th, giving myself a nice long weekend,' one user said.
GTA VI is the latest entry in the franchise and is set to arrive on November 19, more than 13 years after GTA V, the second best–selling video game in history
Another added: 'The last time I took annual leave to play a game on release day was 13 years ago for GTA V... I'm 37 now and just booked two days for GTA VI... Feels good man.'
And one explained: '#GTA6 is not even out yet and management is already playing defense. Anyone calling in sick on Thursday will need an actual doctor's note to be brought in on Friday no exceptions.'
The news comes shortly after broadband operators warned that the imminent release of Grand Theft Auto 6 (GTA VI) could bring the internet to its knees.
Several firms, including BT, are understood to have purchased additional capacity from major internet exchanges in anticipation of a huge surge in traffic when the game launches on November 19.
They have also ramped up their use of caching, restricted scheduled maintenance and stepped up network monitoring to prepare for the influx of data.
'In the lead up to the release, we've seen several ISP [Internet Service Provider] members increase capacity in anticipation of higher demand, demonstrating the resilience and scalability of the UK's internet infrastructure,' said Jennifer Holmes, CEO of the London Internet Exchange.
Although the game won't officially be available until November 19, eager gamers have already begun pre-loading it onto their consoles.
With a whopping file size of 212GB on the PlayStation 5, these early downloads are already placing significant pressure on UK servers – with an even bigger surge in internet traffic expected as the release date draws closer.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine Attacks Kerch Bridge Linking Russia to Occupied Crimea
articles.title_zh: Ukraine Attacks Kerch Bridge Linking Russia to Occupied Crimea
articles.content_orig:
With the SpaceX satellite system faltering, Ukraine’s military launched a surprise, multi-pronged attack to take down vital bridge to Crimea
A t 10pm on Monday evening a Ukrainian soldier scrawled a message on a kamikaze drone. It said simply: “The bridge is fucked.” He then added: “We will stand and Moscow will fall.” It was a freezing night, with a bright starry sky and no clouds. Lines of ice had formed on the drone’s bulky wings. Soon, it would be hurtling towards its target – about 500km to the south.
Typically the soldiers who gathered in this muddy field in central Ukraine were attacking oil refineries deep inside Russia. In recent months the work had become almost mundane: they had hit so many of them. The objective that evening, however, was unique. It was a structure personally associated with Vladimir Putin and his grandiose imperial ambitions.
“We knew what the target was. Everyone was enthusiastic and excited,” one person who took part in the special operation, using the pseudonym “Leon”, told the Guardian. His 7th Deep Strike Centre is part of “Magyar’s Birds”, a brigade named after the call sign of its founder, Robert Brovdi, the head of Ukraine’s unmanned systems forces . Leon said: “Nobody gets excited any more about oil refineries. This was different.”
The soldiers got ready to launch, then watched the biplane-like drone, laden with explosives, disappear across the southern Ukrainian steppe.
Over the next four hours, hundreds of attack drones followed the same linear path, flying first over land and then over the Black Sea. In the early hours of the morning they arrived at their destination: the Kerch bridge connecting occupied Crimea with Russia. Putin opened the monumental road and rail crossing in 2018 , driving across it in a Kamaz truck. This was four years after his undercover troops – known as little green men – seized the peninsula.
Russian propagandists had described the bridge as impregnable. It was, they said, an edifice as strong and unyielding as their country’s iron leader. For Ukraine , by contrast, it was a hated symbol of Russian arrogance and colonial thinking. Also, officials pointed out, it was illegal. Twice Kyiv had tried to blow it up – with a truck bomb in 2022, and a sea drone the following year.
On this occasion, the Ukrainian military’s careful, multi-stage plan worked perfectly. “It was a well-coordinated operation. Waves of drones started from different locations. The goal was to overwhelm Russia’s well-organised air defence system, rather than the bridge itself,” Leon explained.
As expected, the initial salvo tied up Russia’s local defences. According to insiders, Ukraine then launched a second drone wave. Its function was crucial and different: to act as a relay system for radio signals. Previously, Ukrainian units had used Starshield, the military equivalent of Starlink, for mid-range strikes on occupied territory. Elon Musk’s SpaceX owns the satellite internet network, which is overseen by the Pentagon and the Trump administration.
Ten days ago, however, limits were mysteriously imposed on Ukrainian drones, so they could no longer fly at above 161 km/h (100 mph) . SpaceX insists there is no slowdown – a statement Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, says is untrue . On Monday night, it appears Kyiv bypassed US restrictions by setting up its own extraordinary and innovative real-time video and radio connection.
Once the relay was in place, a third wave of attacks could begin. This time they featured Flamingos, a potent Ukrainian-made cruise missile capable of carrying 1,000kg of explosives – enough to seriously damage the bridge. An unknown number of missiles – some reports say at least four – were launched from southern Ukraine and sent towards Crimea.
A video from one of the Flamingos shows it drawing inexorably towards the target. The onboard camera captures a ghostly night-time scene. The crossing looms into view against a grisaille background. Suddenly a gigantic steel arch appears. The feed cuts out. Other footage shows the moment of impact: an orange fireball, pricking the surrounding blackness.
Photos taken on Tuesday morning in the aftermath of the attack show a scene of watery devastation. A massive arch had tumbled overnight into the Kerch straight , with a large concrete chunk of the road crossing. Nobody will be driving across the bridge anytime soon. The adjacent railway arch span was also damaged. “We were very happy, swapping messages all night,” Leon said.
One source in Ukraine’s armed forces said the timing of the operation – hailed by Zelenskyy as “unprecedented” – was deliberate. It was conducted ahead of a meeting on Thursday between Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Putin in the Chinese city of Shenzhen, on the sidelines of an Apec summit. “The bridge is a symbol of Putin’s rule. Destroying it sends a message to the other two great leaders that Putin is not as strong as he pretends,” the person said.
They added: “We understand that what we did shows the world that the king is nude. Putin is weak and vulnerable and we just proved it. The operation was purposefully designed for this specific historic moment. Putin’s plan was to bluff at the summit about how powerful he is. In reality, he can’t even protect the most important and symbolic pillars of his regime.”
In addition to Putin’s political embarrassment before his peers, the disabling of the Kerch bridge has practical consequences. Since annexing Crimea, Russia has militarised the peninsula, effectively turning it into a giant and fortified army base. Since 2022 it has been used as a launch platform for drone and missile attacks on the port of Odesa, and other Ukrainian cities in the region.
Russia’s occupying southern army has relied on the bridge for regular deliveries of ammunition, equipment and fuel. With the crossing partially closed – rail travel reportedly reopened on Tuesday – Russia will have to use an under fire land corridor instead, connecting its Rostov oblast with the Moscow-controlled parts of Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia and Kherson provinces.
“We have disrupted their logistics to Crimea. There will be a lot of problems for Russia’s army in the south,” Leon predicted. Debris from the bridge strike is obstructing the narrow shipping corridor through the Kerch strait, linking the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea. The Azov sea now resembles a lake. Passenger ferries are unable to move, with the occupied ports of Mariupol and Berdyansk cut off.
The soldiers returned from their mission jubilant and elated. Back at their headquarters, they gathered as usual for a minute’s silence, in memory of those killed in Russia’s bloody war. “We had our daily ritual as usual. Then there were congratulations on a very successful and important operation,” Leon said. Then he added: “We are paying them back.”
