articles.title_orig: Nasdaq 100 Futures Rise as Investors Prepare for Nvidia Results
articles.title_zh: Nasdaq 100 Futures Rise as Investors Prepare for Nvidia Results
articles.content_orig:
A major week for Wall Street started on a down note. US markets closed lower Monday, led by declines in technology stocks associated with the artificial intelligence boom.
The S&P 500 fell 1.9%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite fell 2.5%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 739 points, or 1.4%. Wall Street’s fear gauge, the VIX, surged 19%.
Shares of Nvidia ( NVDA ) dropped 4.1%, falling for the third consecutive day since Jensen Huang resigned. Nvidia shares are coming off their worst week in 19 months. Investors are gearing up for Nvidia’s quarterly earnings report, expected Tuesday after the market close.
Shares of the semiconductor chip designer have had a rocky few weeks, with the Huang scandal accelerating declines. Nvidia shares are down roughly 35% since a record high on October 6, erasing about $2 trillion in market value.
On Monday, shares of Nvidia closed at $156.14, their lowest level since July 1, 2025. Nvidia shares have erased all of their gains over the past 16 months. Nvidia stock was hit by a raft of Wall Street analysts slashing their price targets last week. At Evercore ISI, analysts cut their price target to $186, down from a prior target of $465. At HSBC, analysts cut their target to $170, down from $365.
Shares of semiconductor chipmakers, Big Tech and other companies involved in the data center buildout fell Monday. Intel shares ( INTC ) fell 7.1%, while Alphabet shares ( GOOG ) fell 3.85%. CoreWeave shares ( CRWV ) sank 6.1%.
The Commerce Department on Monday also tightened export controls designed to prevent China from accessing sensitive, AI-powering computer chips. The much-anticipated Commerce rule puts new curbs on US exports to data centers that provide “significant volumes” of computing to companies based in countries subject to US arms embargoes, such as China, Iran and Russia.
The Dow, S&P 500 and Nasdaq each gained more than 2% last week. The declines on Monday ate away at those gains. Overall, the S&P and Nasdaq are down roughly 5% and 11%, respectively, since record highs on October 6. The Dow is down 5% since its peak on August 5.
Investors are also gearing up for Anthropic’s expected initial public offering later this week. The AI frontier lab is targeting a valuation of up to $1.4 trillion , and its IPO is a pivotal moment for the tech boom that has become a driving force for the US stock market.
“How investors view Nvidia’s updates against the recent turmoil left in the wake of Jensen Huang’s departure and the market reaction to Anthropic becoming a public company may determine whether the AI trade can gain its footing or whether hiccups here cause further damage across the ecosystem,” Anthony Saglimbene, chief market strategist at Ameriprise Financial, wrote in a Monday note.
This story has been updated with additional content.

articles.content_orig:
Google Wallet is now on iOS and the iPhone . No, you can’t make tap-to-pay payments with Google Wallet or anything like that, but if you store digital versions of your physical cards, they’ll be there.
So yeah, the Google Wallet app is there for scan loyalty cards or your gym membership card and then store for use across Wallet products. You can also manage payment cards and take “control of agentic purchases made across Google.”
Again, though, Google Wallet does not do tap-to-pay, because Apple likely won’t ever let it. Apple wants you to use Apple Pay. Google did note in its announcement that it’s simply not available “at this time,” so they are leaving open the idea that it could one day happen.
Droid Life was started in 2009 and I can't believe we're still here. I've written over 20,000 stories on Android, reviewed thousands of devices, and still find some passion in a dying world of AI.

articles.title_orig: Pentagon detains US soldier accused of spying at British base
articles.title_zh: Pentagon detains US soldier accused of spying at British base
articles.content_orig:
The US military has detained an American soldier accused of spying for Russia at a UK military base.
The senior officer, identified by The Telegraph as Lt Col Brandon Tyner, was first detained by UK counter-terrorism police in Gloucestershire on Nov 10.
On Tuesday, the 41-year-old was taken into custody by the US military over suspected national security and espionage allegations , according to the Metropolitan Police.
Asst Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of counter terrorism policing (CTP) in the UK, said: “Following an extensive investigation, CTP presented our case to the CPS, who in turn engaged with the Attorney General’s Office and American partners. Subsequently, a decision was made to pass the investigation to them to progress.”
He added: “These are extremely serious allegations, and our collective response should send a strong message that we will act swiftly and robustly where we suspect this kind of espionage activity taking place.”
He said UK police would “continue to support our US colleagues as they take the matter forwards”.
Kash Patel, the director of the FBI, said: “This FBI has zero tolerance for anyone who betrays their oath to the United States or puts our national security at risk.”
Lt Col Tyner’s arrest followed a long-running investigation by British and American authorities, including MI5 and the FBI.
It is believed to be the first time a US soldier has been arrested on suspicion of spying offences on British soil.
Lt Col Tyner was assigned to Nato’s Allied Rapid Reaction Corps. He joined the US army in 2008 and served in Iraq, Afghanistan and Qatar, according to a US army official.
The Telegraph understands that he is suspected of sharing intelligence that would be highly damaging in the hands of a foreign power. However, officials are confident that no intelligence left the base.
It is believed that the soldier volunteered his services to Moscow, but was allegedly ensnared by undercover officers posing as Russian operatives.
Officials said his alleged motive was not clear.
He was based at Imjin Barracks in Innsworth, the headquarters of the Nato Allied Rapid Reaction Corps and the UK’s largest Nato base.
Commanded by the British Army, the site hosts service members from more than 20 alliance nations. It holds a readiness force capable of deploying tens of thousands of troops on short notice and recently participated in an exercise modelling the defence of Europe.
An army official said Lt Col Tyner was expected to be prosecuted under the US Uniform Code of Military Justice.
Brig Gen Sean Stinchon, the commander general of the US military’s counter-intelligence command, said: “This case should serve as a stark warning to any service member suspected of violating the oath we all take to protect and defend the Constitution.”
Lt Col Tyner enlisted as a senior human resources officer in January 2008, a military official told The Telegraph.
He earned a bronze star for overseas deployment, having served in Iraq from December 2019 to July 2020, Qatar from July 2016 to July 2017 and Afghanistan from December 2013 to December 2014.
He was promoted to the rank of major in 2018 and lieutenant colonel in 2024.
The serviceman has regularly posted about cryptocurrency online. He also states on his social media that he volunteered at Burning Man festival, and describes himself as a “change agent”.
In his LinkedIn profile, Lt Col Tyner describes himself as a “disruptor” who “thrive[s] in high energy, ever evolving organisations with passions for diversity, growth, and cultural fitness”.

articles.title_orig: There's 'no difference' between buying Anthropic's IPO and Amazon's IPO: Kevin O'Leary
articles.title_zh: There's 'no difference' between buying Anthropic's IPO and Amazon's IPO: Kevin O'Leary
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
As Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ) prepares to begin trading under the ticker ANT on Thursday, Nov. 19, business leaders are weighing in on the historically large initial public offering (IPO).
"There's no difference in investing in Anthropic on the IPO than Amazon on its IPO," "Shark Tank" host and O'Leary Ventures chair Kevin O'Leary said on Sozzi Unleashed . "There was tremendous volatility. It made zero money. But look at the platform it ultimately built. That's what you're betting on in the Anthropic deal."
Sitting down with Yahoo Finance's Brian Sozzi, O'Leary said the past few years haven't been great for buying IPOs, but he believes Anthropic may be a unique way to bet on artificial intelligence.
Anthropic said it expects to sell 825 million shares priced between $70 and $78 each. That would give the company a market valuation of between $1.3 trillion and $1.45 trillion — putting it near SpaceX's ( SPCX ) IPO valuation of $1.77 trillion, which was the largest ever.
Read more: Everything you need to know ahead of Anthropic's IPO
"It may be the most hyped IPO ever," O'Leary said. "This IPO is the anchor to the entire AI or SI trade, whatever you want to call it."
What about the fact that Anthropic may not turn a profit until 2030? Though Anthropic's operating losses have improved, they still total $1.3 billion for the first nine months of the year. The company also noted in its amended IPO filing that it plans to spend nearly $900 billion on computing and data centers, with $70 billion of that total coming due within a year.
O'Leary said Anthropic's profitability is the wrong lens right now. Buying in is a bet on AI's role across all 11 sectors of the economy, and he sees evidence of productivity and margin gains so far. That has helped markets remain near all-time highs despite tariffs, wars, and high energy prices.
These remarks follow O'Leary's comments last month, when the businessman called Anthropic "a hot trade."
"I expect it to be liquid from day one, and that changes the opportunity," he wrote in October.

articles.title_zh: Sean Duffy’s attacks on past FAA ground stop resurface
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON — The Trump administration’s request for $50.1 billion in new Federal Aviation Administration funding after a nationwide ground stop strangled air travel is running into skepticism from both parties on Capitol Hill.
The funding request was suddenly increased from $30 billion after the hourslong ground stop Friday caused delays and cancellations for passengers across thousands of flights.
The formal funding ask was conveyed in a Tuesday letter signed by Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, who refused to apologize or accept responsibility for the failure, blaming it on predecessors and Congress. The letter, cosigned by FAA chief Bryan Bedford and White House budget director Russell Vought, stated the money was needed “to deliver a truly world-class air traffic control network.”
After publicly reproaching Congress for the failure last week, Duffy met privately with Senate Republicans on Tuesday to make his case on Capitol Hill.
The closed-door briefing was contentious. The transportation secretary was “yelled at” by multiple Republican senators during his briefing, according to a person in the room who was not authorized to speak publicly about the private discussion.
When it was over, Senate Republican leaders and Duffy notably held their news conferences separately.
Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., stopped short of endorsing the full funding figure, saying only that the GOP is unified around the belief that “safe skies is an incredibly important priority.”
“We will see what the traffic will bear, what’s achievable,” he said, calling it a “discussion to be had” on the dollar amount.
Duffy met with only Republicans on Tuesday, not Democrats — even though the regular government funding process requires bipartisan support.
And Democrats were left wanting a better explanation, particularly as Duffy has pointed fingers at them. And members in both parties noted that President Donald Trump’s “big, beautiful bill” included $12.5 billion for air traffic control that still has not been fully used up.
“Look, we have not been given the answers. They have not come clean,” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., told reporters on Tuesday. “At his first press conference, all Duffy did was attack Democrats, and he asked for $50 billion when they haven’t even spent the $12 billion we’ve given to them. I have little faith in them.”
Facing Republican questions on the matter, Duffy insisted that the $12.5 billion was insufficient for the specific upgrades he deemed necessary in this situation.
Other Democrats are vexed by the FAA funding request.
“I generally support the idea of investing in air traffic control, but $50 billion sounds like an awfully round number,” said Sen. Brian Schatz, D-Hawaii, who’s poised to become majority whip and also sits on the Senate Appropriations Committee.
The issue is wrapped up in a larger debate about funding the government ahead of a Dec. 11 deadline to avoid another shutdown . Congress could either reach a deal by then on new funding, punt it to next year with a stopgap bill, or fail to act and allow a shutdown.
Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, said air traffic control is “absolutely not a partisan issue” and that Congress will work to make sure that any funding is “paid for in a responsible way.”
Republicans are also considering a party-line “reconciliation” bill to approve military funding without the need for Democratic votes; Democrats are likely to resist additional military funds unless the Iran war comes to an end. Other provisions could be added to such a bill — if it materializes before Republicans lose control of Congress. Thune indicated Tuesday that it is still an open question, as Republicans would need to pass a budget resolution by Thanksgiving to pull it off. It would be a long, arduous process requiring near-total GOP unity in both chambers, and it would need to begin soon in order to finish this year.
Duffy said he’s agnostic on how the funds get passed when asked by NBC News why he only met with Republicans on Tuesday.
“I have met with Democrats. I’ve spent hours on the phone with Democrats. Get along with them well. They understand this issue,” Duffy said Tuesday, speaking to reporters separately after meeting with GOP senators. “I’m not going to tell them how to do their work, but I’m telling everybody what we need. I’m making a nice ask, and I’m going to let them work their process.”
One of the Democrats whom Duffy spoke to was House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., the likely next House speaker.
“I appreciated the conversation,” Jeffries told reporters. “There are still more questions than answers in terms of what happened, why it happened, how do we prevent it from happening again.”
Jeffries added that he wants a briefing on the FAA ground stop and other recent outages, saying: “These developments are troubling, and it’s unclear if it’s all infrastructure-related or whether there’s some malignant activity.”
When asked about Duffy’s $50.1 billion request, outgoing House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., said Republicans would work with the administration to fund “as much of that as we can.” He pointed to the $12.5 billion already approved for FAA modernization and did not specify a timeline or whether Congress would pursue a supplemental funding package.
I am a field producer for NBC News based in Washington, D.C., covering all things politics.
Sahil Kapur is a senior national political reporter for NBC News.
Julie Tsirkin is a correspondent covering Capitol Hill and the White House.

articles.title_orig: California DMV bans Waymos from operating on state freeways after series of traffic incidents
articles.title_zh: California DMV bans Waymos from operating on state freeways after series of traffic incidents
articles.content_orig:
Some of the incidents reportedly involve Waymos in active construction zones.
The California Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) has ordered Waymo to stop operating its autonomous vehicles on California freeways, citing concerns that the vehicles pose an imminent public safety hazard.
The DMV's decision follows a series of incidents involving Waymo vehicles on Bay Area freeways, specifically citing two of them.
One of the incidents noted by the agency involved three Waymo vehicles that entered an active construction zone on U.S. Highway 101 near Burlingame, putting workers, equipment and other vehicles at risk. According to the DMV, similar incidents have occurred multiple times.
The other incident cited by the DMV drew additional attention after video showed a Waymo vehicle attempting to pass California Highway Patrol patrol cars conducting a traffic break on Interstate 280 earlier this month.
In a statement, Waymo said safety remains its top priority.
"Our ride-hailing service continues to operate safely on surface streets, serving over half a million trips each week. We are working with the California DMV and other state officials diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations," a spokesperson told our sister station in the Bay Area.
SEE ALSO: California passenger stuck inside self-driving Waymo car through construction zone, followed by police
The DMV said concerns about Waymo vehicles on freeways are not new.
This is the second time this year Waymo has faced freeway restrictions. In May 2026, Waymo said it was pausing freeway operations in several cities, including San Francisco and Los Angeles, to improve how its vehicles respond in construction zones.
The California DMV says the new restrictions went into effect on Nov. 11 and "will remain in place until Waymo demonstrates to the department that it has taken effective corrective actions..."
"I see this as an opportunity to continue improving a technology," said Billy Riggs, a professor at the University of San Francisco.
Riggs said data shows autonomous vehicles remain safer than human drivers overall, but added that challenges are expected as the technology continues to develop.
"An automated vehicle can understand and identify all the aspects of the roadway and make really sophisticated judgments on them. But, many times, it can't understand context," Riggs said.
Earlier this year, San Francisco resident Elliot Slade said he was riding in a Waymo vehicle when it went off course and entered a construction zone. KGO-TV, our sister station in the Bay Area, previously spoke with Slade about the incident and interviewed him again on Monday.
"I used to use it all the time, and now it's like, eh, I'll walk or I'll take the (bus)," Slade said.
Slade said the experience left him skeptical about using Waymo vehicles in the future. While he acknowledged that accidents can happen with any vehicle, he said he remains concerned about the potential consequences if similar incidents continue.
"You had one chance to fix it if it went viral. And if they haven't made sure it's completely safe, then I'm disappointed. Super disappointed," Slade said.

articles.title_orig: Apple, Google and more services down in latest wave of widespread outages
articles.title_zh: Apple, Google and more services down in latest wave of widespread outages
articles.content_orig:
Apple said it was experiencing tech issues Tuesday that were affecting several of its popular consumer-facing services.
As of 2 p.m. ET, Apple’s own system status page showed that Apple Business, Apple School Manager, AppleCare, iCloud Mail and Web Apps, and SchoolWork were each experiencing outages.
Stream Philadelphia News for free, 24/7, wherever you are with NBC10.
Earlier, the page showed the App Store and Apple Music experiencied outages.
“Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning,” an Apple spokesperson told NBC News. “We’re working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible.”
At Apple stores in New York and Chicago, employees told NBC News earlier in the day that their internal software had stopped working and they had been unable to complete purchases or make appointments.
Marriott International, the largest U.S. hotel operator, was also having technology issues that guests reported had impacted reservations and check-ins, among other problems, according to users posting on Reddit. Downdetector.com also reported that Marriott was experiencing an outage.
Marriott, which has 10,200 properties and more than 1.8 million rooms under its corporate umbrella, did not immediately respond to a request for comment from the Associated Press.
Gmail also appeared to experience an outage briefly Tuesday, with some users reporting issues accessing their email, according to Downdetector. The issue did not appear to be widespread and the company posted on X that they weren't "currently seeing evidence of a broad Gmail service disruption."
The outages come on the heels of a string of major disruptions impacting U.S. services over the past several days — including Monday's Chase, Bank of America and Wells Fargo banking disruptions and United Airlines departing-flight system glitch , following Friday's nationwide FAA ground stop and Thursday's Microsoft cloud outage.
President Donald Trump brushed off the recent outages that wreaked havoc on air travel, banks and emails, saying Tuesday, “it’s life.”
“It’s life, it’s life,” he told reporters during his trip to the Philippines when asked about the outages. “When you’re big and powerful and you have all the money, things like that happen. It’s fine.”
While none of the issues appear to be related, they’ve exposed America’s reliance on older infrastructure and revealed the extent to which companies and governments are being forced to upgrade systems in the AI age. The incidents have also stoked unfounded paranoia that something larger may be afoot.

articles.title_orig: The data is very preliminary, but Vulcan failure may not be due to BE-4 engines
articles.title_zh: The data is very preliminary, but Vulcan failure may not be due to BE-4 engines
articles.content_orig:
United Launch Alliance (ULA) confirmed Tuesday morning that its return-to-flight launch of the Vulcan rocket began failing during the initial stages of the mission.
“While we appear to have lost telemetry and the mission at approximately 10 minutes into flight, early indications are that just after liftoff, the launch vehicle experienced low booster performance, resulting in stage separation occurring when the vehicle was low in altitude and below minimal velocity to reach orbit,” the company said .
The launch company also confirmed reporting by Ars that the Centaur V upper stage and the solid rocket boosters performed nominally during the flight.
Critically, ULA did not provide any specific information about the “low booster performance.” This matters greatly because the core stage of the Vulcan rocket is powered by two BE-4 engines, which are provided by Blue Origin. That company’s own New Glenn rocket uses a similar but slightly more powerful version of the BE-4 engine. And New Glenn experienced its own catastrophic failure in May during a ground test, a failure that later was attributed to a main oxygen valve on one of the BE-4 engines.
Information about the Vulcan failure is being closely held by ULA and Blue Origin, who have only acknowledged that they’re working together to investigate the cause. According to two sources, the investigation is “incredibly complicated” and remains in the early stages.
However, according to preliminary data, two independent sources indicated to Ars that the problem is currently believed to have originated on the launch vehicle side rather than in the engines themselves. The issue may be related to systems that feed methane and liquid oxygen propellant to the engines.
ULA engineers are looking at the possibility that one of the two BE-4 engines started producing lower thrust shortly after liftoff and never ramped back up to full throttle for the remainder of the burn. Video observations from high-zoom tracking cameras appeared to show one engine slightly dimmer than the other after Vulcan jettisoned its solid rocket boosters nearly two minutes into flight. An asymmetric shutdown of the BE-4 engines could also have contributed to the sudden attitude motion indicated by ULA’s telemetry-driven real-time animation near stage separation.
The Federal Aviation Administration is overseeing the investigation, which is being led by ULA. Again, this information is preliminary, and no definitive conclusions can or should be drawn.
This was the fifth flight of the Vulcan rocket since its debut in January 2024. Two of the previous flights have experienced issues with the nozzles on its solid rocket boosters, but in both cases, the rocket was able to compensate for the reduced and asymmetric thrust and reach its intended orbit. The second nozzle issue caused Vulcan to stand down for nine months.
This latest setback is likely to sideline Vulcan for at least half a year, and probably longer. Most impacted will be the US Space Force, which has national security payloads waiting for a ride to space on Vulcan, and Amazon, which had more than a dozen launches of its Amazon Leo constellation on the manifest for 2027. It would exacerbate a worsening launch crisis in the United States.
There are potentially serious implications for Blue Origin as well, which is seeking to return New Glenn to flight as early as January. Last Tuesday, the company said a modified BE-4 main oxygen valve had successfully completed qualification testing.
“Our modified valve has already been incorporated into engines slated for upcoming flights, and we are now rolling it out across the remaining fleet,” the company said . “We expect to complete the anomaly investigation later this month.”
If Vulcan’s failure were ultimately due to a problem with the BE-4 engine, it would certainly delay the New Glenn rocket’s return to flight. This would be a setback not just for Blue Origin but for NASA, which is counting on the super heavy lift rocket to do much of the heavy lifting for its Artemis Program and Moon Base.

articles.title_orig: Is Apple down? Thousands report problems accessing services
articles.title_zh: Is Apple down? Thousands report problems accessing services
articles.content_orig:
Apple said an internal update was to blame for a major outage on Nov. 17 that hit its App Store, iCloud, Apple Pay and other software, with thousands of users reporting problems online.
In a statement to USA TODAY, Apple said it was working to fix the affected systems, and services are expected to return to normal soon.
"Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning. We're working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible," the company said.
Apple, on its System Status page , confirmed outages on App Store, Apple Music and AppleCare on Device, as well as issues with iCloud Account & Sign In. The company told Bloomberg the problems weren't caused by a cyberattack.
According to outage tracker Downdetector, reports of issues with Apple Pay began to spike at around 11:40 a.m. ET with a peak of reports at around 12:15 p.m. ET. Outage reports for iCloud also started to surge just before noon ET, though reports on Downdetector don't reflect every user experiencing a problem. Those reports had dropped significantly by mid-afternoon.
The Apple software issues came on the heels of a major banking outage on Nov. 16 that stemmed from Chase Bank. It also impacted Wells Fargo, Bank of America, online payment platform Zelle and other institutions.
Last week, a communications outage disrupted air traffic across the United States, and a Microsoft outage prevented many from checking their Outlook email and accessing Microsoft 365 services like Teams and Word.

By MELISSA KOENIG, US REPORTER and ASSOCIATED PRESS
Published: 17:12 EST, 16 November 2026 | Updated: 08:04 EST, 17 November 2026
United Airlines flights across the United States were grounded on Monday night, just days after a technical issue prompted the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to ground all flights nationwide.
The airline announced on social media that it was experiencing a 'widespread system outage' as it apologized to customers 'for the inconvenience.'
'We're aware of the widespread system and our teams are working hard to get things back up and running as soon as possible,' it posted on X.
'We appreciate your patience while we work through this,' the airline added, urging anyone with scheduled flights to keep checking their flight status on the app.
The post has since been deleted, as a spokesperson for the airline told the Daily Mail that the issue has been resolved.
'While some flights were delayed, there was no impact on flights in progress, or on United Express flights,' the spokesperson said, adding: 'There is no indication that this was a cybersecurity-related issue.'
The update came after frustrated travelers took to social media to bemoan how their flights could not take off.
'Currently stuck on the tarmac,' one X user posted, blaming it on an IT issue in which the airline 'can't clear planes for takeoff as [they] can't connect to the weight system.'
United Airlines flights across the country were grounded Monday night as the airline experienced a 'widespread system outage'
The issue comes just days after a technical issue prompted the Federal Aviation Administration to ground all flights nationwide
United Airlines said on social media its teams were 'working hard to get things back up and running as soon as possible'
The outage is now the latest in a string of technical issues that have crippled businesses around the country and left airline passengers stranded for hours amid a rare nationwide ground stop.
Earlier Monday, thousands of customers with Chase, Bank of America, Capital One and Wells Fargo also flagged being unable to log in or transfer money , according to Down Detector, a website which tracks real-time user reports.
A spokesperson for Chase told the Daily Mail the outage was caused by a technical bug.
'Due to a technical issue, some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete but customers still have access to their accounts and funds,' they said. 'We are working to resolve this as quickly as possible.'
Chase also addressed one complaint on X, telling a client: 'I do apologize, it appears that we are currently working to resolve an issue with online banking.
'Please try again at a later time. We're sorry for any inconvenience, and appreciate your patience.'
Wells Fargo also posted a note on its website telling customers that 'online banking isn't available right now' due to 'technical issues'.
A spokesperson for Chase later noted that the technical problems were not the result of a cyberattack.
'JPMorgan Chase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in an on-premise hardware system - it is not cyber-related,' said spokesman Joe Evangelisti.
In the same statement, Evangelisti said that this was a Chase-only issue.
'This is not a systemic issue - other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us,' he said.
Customers at three major US banks have been locked out of their accounts as Chase and Wells Fargo all experienced outages on Monday afternoon
Over 20,000 flights were canceled from Friday to Sunday, according to airline tracker FlightAware. During that same period, over 25,000 flights were delayed, and lingering impacts have bled into Monday
A spokesman for US Bank said its systems were not directly impacted but that 'clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays.'
Zelle is the peer-to-peer payment system that major US banks use to allow customers to send money to friends and family at near-instant speed.
It is owned by Arizona-based Early Warning Services, which in turn is owned by financial institutions including Bank of America, Capital One, JPMorgan Chase, PNC Bank, Truist, US Bank and Wells Fargo.
A spokesman for Early Warning Services said the Zelle network was fully operational.
'An issue at the financial institutions may be delaying Zelle payments for some of their customers,' the spokesman said.
Still, the outage sparked panic as it came just three days after Microsoft experienced widespread issues on Friday , leaving people unable to access Outlook, Teams and Copilot applications.
Businesses ground to a halt, healthcare providers lost contact with patients, courts lost live feeds, and governments struggled to communicate.
The suspected cause was a faulty network configuration change that resulted in numerous servers becoming unavailable, overloading the remaining infrastructure.
The FAA also issued a rare nationwide ground stop at all US airports following a major communications failure on Friday.
'What you saw on Friday was very, very old equipment that had a heart attack,' Trump said on Monday of the FAA outage that forced thousands of cancelled and delayed flights over the weekend
The Air Traffic Control System Command Center (ATCSCC) said on Friday that the  halting of 3,500 US flights for five hours was 'due to extraordinary circumstances for safety reasons'.
'There has been a temporary telecommunications outage - out of an abundance of caution, all flights have been halted,' the FAA said.
'Every flight has been accounted for, and international flights will be handled on a case-by-case basis.'
President Donald Trump has since blamed half-century-old aviation equipment for the ground stop, which led to thousands of cancellations and travel woes for over a million passengers.
'We have old, broken equipment,' the President said Monday at the White House before departing for his trip to Asia on board the new Air Force One plane gifted to the administration by Qatari officials.
He noted that some of the equipment that went down was 55 years old.
'We essentially want to blow it up and put new in, and we can do it simultaneously with very little trouble. What you saw on Friday was very, very old equipment that had a heart attack.'
The incident marked only the second time since the 9/11 terrorist attacks that a nationwide ground stop was implemented.
The stoppage also prevented any domestic flights from taking off, resulting in one of the worst travel snarls in recent US history. It began around 3.30pm and was not lifted until around 8.20pm.
More than 20,000 flights were canceled from Friday to Sunday, according to airline tracker FlightAware. During that same period, over 25,000 flights were delayed, and lingering impacts have bled into Monday.
It is estimated that more than one million American travelers have been impacted by the outage.
Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy claimed Biden-era upgrades were shoddy
The President also cast blame on his predecessor for the FAA glitch.
'The Biden administration hooked up a lot of copper into glass. And copper, if you know anything about electrical engineering, you cannot hook up copper into glass. So a lot of money was wasted, but the equipment is very old,' Trump said.
He was referring to Biden-era upgrades to communication systems built on copper wiring that were upgraded to fiber-optic, or glass, wires.
Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said the upgrade work was shoddy, resulting in the outage.
Trump said the upgrade was a waste of money and more cash would be needed from Congress to fully upgrade the system and prevent future issues.
'We want to make it beyond safe. We want to have the best system in the world, and for that we need Congress,' the President told reporters.

articles.title_orig: Three China-related Items to Consider as Trump Again Meets with Xi
articles.title_zh: Three China-related Items to Consider as Trump Again Meets with Xi
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
SEOUL — President Trump will get his wish for a historic meeting among the three most powerful men in the world — Xi Jinping of China, Vladimir Putin of Russia and himself — at a summit Thursday in southern China.
But Moscow, Beijing and Washington already know their leaders are arriving at the Shenzhen conference with disparate aims.
Trump hopes to focus the meeting on nuclear nonproliferation, urging the Russian and Chinese presidents to work with him to scale back the world’s largest nuclear stockpiles. Putin pressed for the meeting to discuss his ongoing war in Ukraine . And Xi wants to discuss neither, only embracing the idea of the summit to show the world China can help broker peace on the international stage, Chinese officials told The Times.
“That’ll be interesting,” Trump said earlier this week,  teasing the trilateral summit before the White House formally confirmed the meeting Friday.
“We’re talking a lot of things, including denuclearization,” he added, “but we’ll be talking a lot of things.”
U.S. officials have acknowledged they do not expect the meeting to result in a breakthrough on arms control. China is openly racing to build up its nuclear capacity — a nonnegotiable policy in Beijing, which sees its arsenal dwarfed by an American stockpile nearly 10 times the size.
“We do not expect to get to any kind of agreement. I would characterize this as the entry point,” one senior Trump administration official said. “This is the beginning of hopefully a conversation that can be productive going forward.”
Trump’s break from long-standing tradition in U.S.-Russia relations was real, but it should not have been entirely surprising.
The Chinese, too, threw cold water on the chances of a breakthrough, with one Chinese official telling The Times the central government saw no benefit to a pause.
“It is a matter of survival,” the official said.
The United States and Russia still command the world’s two dominant nuclear arsenals, with over 5,000 warheads each. China has an estimated 620 — but in catching up, it is developing new warheads with more sophisticated delivery systems.
Moscow, too, is modernizing its weapons, after the Trump administration allowed the last major U.S.-Russian nuclear arms treaty to expire earlier this year.
Though expectations are low for a nuclear breakthrough, Trump doesn’t want to discuss Putin’s priorities, either, the U.S. official added.
“He does not intend to talk about Ukraine in that meeting,” the official said. “China is not really part of that track, so it doesn’t really seem appropriate.”
Ukraine has grown increasingly concerned by Trump’s pressure campaign to force it into concessions to Moscow as he pushes to end the war.
The Trump administration has brought Russian and Ukrainian officials together at a working level to explore the viability of peace talks. But a long-standing U.S. policy on the war — not to negotiate about Ukraine without Ukraine — could be further compromised at a trilateral with Putin and Xi.
The only American business leader confirmed to join Trump in Asia is Elon Musk, the Tesla and SpaceX chief who was seen as instrumental in the decision last month to restrict Ukraine’s access on the battlefield to Starlink , the satellite internet service owned by Musk.
Beijing has struck a careful balance on Ukraine, publicly issuing its respect for sovereign borders — a position popular among Chinese voices who support Kyiv — while giving Moscow diplomatic cover, an economic lifeline and technological support throughout the war.
The summit’s stark lack of substance surprised even the closest China watchers.
Their competing agendas could make the summit little more than a spectacle, yet still produce images that hark back to the famous Yalta Conference — held in Crimea, the Ukrainian peninsula currently occupied by Russia, in 1945 — where Josef Stalin, Franklin Delano Roosevelt and Winston Churchill carved up a postwar order.
The summit on Chinese soil offers Xi a powerful image to broadcast worldwide , demonstrating an emergent superpower can bring together the leaders of two historic rivals in the name of peace.
Putin gets to present himself as a global player, despite the devastation wrought on Russia’s economy and military standing after four bruising years of war.
And it allows Trump to reassert his global relevance after this month’s midterms delivered the worst electoral rebuke to a president in half a century, rivaling the backlash against President Nixon during Watergate.

articles.title_orig: FAA pauses installation of new routers after ground stop
articles.title_zh: FAA pauses installation of new routers after ground stop
articles.content_orig:
The Federal Aviation Administration said Tuesday it would pause the installation of new routers after problems with the technology led the agency to issue a rare nationwide ground stop on Friday.
Tens of thousands of flights were affected by the ground stop, which halted departing flights for more than four hours. It was the longest halt to U.S. flight departures since 9/11.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Sunday that an overloaded router installed in southern Arkansas as part of an upgrade to a system overseen by L3Harris Technologies appeared to overwhelm systems that feed radar and other data for air traffic control.
The Wall Street Journal first reported the news about the pause.
The FAA and Department of Transportation have said L3Harris was working to convert the communications network from copper wires to fiber optic.
Democratic members of the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science and Transportation this week asked the FAA and the Department of Transportation for clarity on what went wrong.
"Identifying the device that failed does not establish why it failed," the senators wrote in a statement. "Modernization cannot come at the expense of operational safety."
The agencies have said they are working to figure out the root cause of the issue and have reiterated that there is no indication of a cyberattack or outside threat.
The senators also asked for a briefing with the FAA, L3Harris and Juniper Networks, which is making the new devices, by Monday. They asked the companies to lay out why the operational systems lacked sufficient redundancy and answer other questions about what led to the outage.
CNBC has reached out to L3Harris and Juniper Networks for comment.
Duffy on Friday called for Congress to approve $50 billion in funding for upgrades to the aging U.S. air traffic control system, more than he has previously asked for. Democratic lawmakers pushed back on the request, citing unspent money from existing funding, which includes Congress' approval last year of $12.5 billion for airport and air traffic control improvements over five years.
Senate Commerce Chair Ted Cruz, R-Texas, said Tuesday that he thinks there will be support for air traffic control modernization, but that the allocation should be specifically for safety upgrades.
"I don't think the full $50 billion will be funded," he said. "Some of that is not safety related, but we just discussed there, and what I expressed is that the request needs to be focused on safety modernization."
Aging equipment and a shortage of air traffic controllers have for years angered airline executives, who have complained about the cost of resulting disruptions.
— CNBC's Phil LeBeau , Leslie Josephs and Justin Papp contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Kalshi takes down controversial Trump 'mention' markets at CFTC's request
articles.title_zh: Kalshi takes down controversial Trump 'mention' markets at CFTC's request
articles.content_orig:
Prediction market platform Kalshi quietly paused trading in a handful of "mention" contracts tied to President Donald Trump at the end of last week at the request of the CFTC, the company confirmed on Tuesday.
Mention markets are made up of contracts that ask traders what specific words will be used in a speech, a corporate earnings call or during a television broadcast.  Earlier this year, a White House teleprompter operator used inside information to place trades in mention markets related to the president's comments.
Markets paused include those asking traders what nicknames Trump will say before 2027, what the president will say in November and what countries and companies Trump will say before the end of the month.
The move comes after the Commodity Futures Trading Commission , the federal agency overseeing prediction markets, said in a letter to exchanges in September that mentions contracts have a greater manipulation risk.
A spokesperson for the agency told CNBC that the commission has placed holds on the certification of some of Kalshi's proposed mention markets. The spokesperson cited a Kalshi contract on hold that asked what key words would Trump say before a certain date. The contract was originally self-certified by Kalshi in February 2025.
"The CFTC stayed the certification of these contracts because they may be susceptible to manipulation, which is consistent with the staff advisory the CFTC put out two months ago," said Brooke Nethercott, the agency's spokesperson.
In a statement, Kalshi spokesperson Dani Lever said Kalshi is complying with the order.
In August, reports emerged that the CFTC was conducting an internal review into mention markets. The agency also requested that Kalshi, which is the only U.S.-regulated exchange that features the contract type, take down its sports-related mention markets in response to the inquiry. Kalshi complied.
A Trump-related mention market drew scrutiny in July after it was revealed a White House teleprompter operator placed trades on markets related to the president's comments. In a settlement with the operator, the CFTC ordered a three-year trading ban on the individual and a penalty amounting to over $172,000 .
Kalshi has defended mentions markets even as the CFTC has become increasingly skeptical of them, saying that the individual words of prominent people often cause billions of dollars of movement across financial markets.
In addition to scrutiny regarding mention markets, the company is also facing a probe from the CFTC about its communications about new products with the agency, though a spokesperson for the company told CNBC that it was working to resolve the issues.
As of Tuesday morning, a mention market asking what Vice President JD Vance would say during the New York Times DealBook Summit event on Wednesday is still active.
Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

articles.title_zh: Why Russia and China aren't really best friends
articles.content_orig:
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Russia's growing dependence on China is reshaping one of the world's most important geopolitical relationships. Since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the resulting Western sanctions, Russia has relied heavily on Beijing for trade, technology and critical imports. Along the vast Russia-China border, economic cooperation is expanding, but experts warn that the relationship is increasingly unequal, giving China significant leverage.
DW explores historical tensions, Russian security concerns, reports of espionage and the strategic risks facing Russia as China's influence grows, raising questions about the future of the countries' much-publicized "no-limits" partnership.

articles.title_orig: How new US chip restrictions on South East Asia will hit China
articles.title_zh: How new US chip restrictions on South East Asia will hit China
articles.content_orig:
As US President Donald Trump heads to China, his administration has renewed efforts to curb Beijing's access to advanced semiconductors.
On Monday, Washington announced new interim rules that will increase scrutiny of  data centre operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil.
The move not only restricts the export of advanced chips, but also access to their computing power, which Chinese firms currently rent abroad to train artificial intelligence (AI) models.
South East Asian countries in particular have invested heavily in data centres to power their AI ambitions - and Chinese firms seeking computing power overseas have been a key market.
But now these firms will need a US government licence to buy advanced chips from Nvidia or other American chipmakers. This allows Washington to monitor if those chips are being used to serve Chinese companies, or being smuggled to China.
This poses a fresh challenge for Beijing, which has become deeply dependent on compute from abroad in the wake of US export restrictions. At least 30% of China's advanced AI computing power is projected to come from renting overseas or smuggling in 2027, according to research by the Institute for Progress , a US-based think-tank.
China's foreign ministry called the new rules "economic coercion" and said Beijing "will take necessary measures to firmly safeguard its own legitimate rights and interests".
This is also a problem for South East Asian economies where large numbers of data centres have sprung up recently. Some of the firms behind them are accused of helping China evade US export controls on advanced chips.
One of those is Singaporean data centre firm Megaspeed, whose former director Alice Huang is suspected of being a Chinese spy. Calls for tighter export controls have grown after Nvidia's Jensen Huang admited to an affair with her and resigned as CEO .
Megaspeed, the biggest buyer of Nvidia's chips in South East Asia, is accused of illegally smuggling chips to Chinese companies after purchasing them for use in data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.
The company has denied these allegations, defended its business as "legitimate and lawful", and said it has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation". It also said Alice Huang stepped down from her role as director in late 2023 and left the firm last year.
The US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, however, has said Brazil and the four South East Asian nations "present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion" of the chips that Washington wants to keep out of China's hands.
The new measures are aimed at ensuring sensitive US technology "cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries," the bureau added. Licences will be issued on a "case-by-case basis", it said.
Countries like Malaysia and Thailand whose data centre roll out has been heavily driven by Chinese buyers could be hit hardest, says international trade expert Naoise McDonagh from Australia's Edith Cowan University.
But the new rules are unlikely to derail the data centre boom as a whole, says Reema Bhattacharya from advisory firm Verisk Maplecroft, adding that investment backed by major tech firms and clearly identifiable customers should "remain relatively resilient".
Singapore was an early adopter of data centres but when it began limiting new construction, investment flowed to neighbours Malaysia and Thailand. Johor in Malaysia and Batam in Indonesia have also approved billions of dollars worth of data centres to catch the spillover demand.
These countries have been offering incentives such as cheaper land to attract foreign investment, including from Chinese tech giants Alibaba and Tencent.
But now, the region could find it harder to get hold of advanced chips.
The BBC has contacted Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand for comment.
Singapore said it is "engaging relevant US authorities" to understand the new rules better, and is "exploring how to facilitate trusted access" for local firms.
A spokesperson for Brazil's Ministry of Development, Industry, Trade and Services said it is aware of the US announcement and it "is closely monitoring any potential developments regarding this measure".
Malaysia previously said it welcomes data centre investment but "will not allow itself to be used to get around export controls".
The new rules also come just ahead of Trump's meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Shenzhen this week.
Beijing has made self-sufficiency in tech a national priority and needs the best chips to build powerful AI models.
Chinese firms DeepSeek and MoonShot have come close to US rivals like Anthropic and OpenAI. So much so that The Institute for Progress estimates top US AI models lead the best Chinese platforms by only about six and half months.
"This is despite US AI companies having significantly better compute access and financing," it said.
Still, China needs advanced US chips to ensure its best AI models are competitive, experts tell the BBC.
The new restrictions on South East Asia and Brazil have taken away "one of the more practical routes Chinese AI developers had to accessing frontier computing power," Bhattacharya said.
But tighter restrictions could also push Chinese firms towards domestic semiconductors and further drive advancement at home.
That has been a longstanding dilemma for Washington, McDonagh said: whether to keep selling chips to China to retain its reliance on the US, or restrict access and risk further spurring Chinese innovation.

articles.title_orig: Grok Bot took unapproved actions, ignored orders to stop, and then denied it
articles.title_zh: Grok Bot took unapproved actions, ignored orders to stop, and then denied it
articles.content_orig:
Researchers recently discovered unexpected behavior from Grok Bot, the AI agent platform from Elon Musk’s SpaceXSI. Over five days, Grok bots installed on two separate employee laptops made 31 requests to access data stored in employee calendar, email, Slack, and GitHub accounts. The bots performed the actions even though the employees had never ordered them and continued doing them even after employees instructed them to stop. The bots also denied having taken the actions at all.
The behavior was reported Tuesday by NewCore, the maker of a managed gateway product that acts as an intermediary between AI agents and the tools and accounts they are assigned to work with. In some cases, the unapproved access attempts occurred while the laptop with Grok Bot installed had its lid shut, or late at night while the employee was sleeping. None of the unprompted actions were recorded in Grok logs. Without the gateway logs, the employees would have had no idea they occurred. And of course, without the gateway, the unapproved accesses would have succeeded—again without the end user’s knowledge.
Once the employees learned that Grok Bot had tried to check in with accounts without prompting, one of them instructed the agent, four separate times, to stop taking any actions on its own. The agent’s reply was: “I won’t set that up, and I’ll stop offering recurring check-ins.” Despite acknowledging the explicit instructions, the Grok Bot made more unapproved access attempts. When one of the employees asked the bot if it made any accesses, it checked twice and then outputted: “Overnight into Friday morning I was idle.”
The NewCore employees sent the gateway logs to Grok Bot support personnel and asked what was causing the bots to access accounts without prompting or approval. The support team’s reply indicated the behavior was by design and intended to allow the bots to proactively take actions on behalf of users. In other words, the unrequested and unlogged access attempts were a feature designed to make Grok Bot more useful by periodically checking in and finding tasks to perform before a user even asks. The proactive check-in is a feature of Cursor, the AI coding service SpaceXSI recently acquired.
“There is no bug to patch, which is exactly why this is worse than a bug,” Ido Hoorvitch, a NewCore security researcher, wrote in an email. “A vulnerability gets fixed. This is the product working as designed: an agent that holds your credentials, acts under your identity while you sleep, ignores the one refusal you can give it, and then tells you it did nothing.”
Hoorvitch said that Grok Bot provides minimal notification of the automatic “turns,” or the cycles that occur when an agent receives instructions or context, decides what to do, and calls whatever tools it chooses. The notice comes during onboarding when the bot says it keeps working while the user is away from the computer and connects to apps and uses them the way the user does.
“It reads like a welcome message and scrolls off the screen in under a minute,” Hoorvitch said. “Nobody is asked to consent to it. Nothing says the platform will start turns with no message from you, or that those turns will use your connectors.”
The researcher said that Grok Bot documentation notes that a primary bot checks in on its own, and a changelog mentions brief background wakes, but there is no mention that the check-ins “reach into your connected apps.” Further, once a check-in runs, there is no mention of it in the chat interface or in the chat history, and as already noted, prompts to stop check-ins don’t work. Hoorvitch said the bot “always asks before making changes,” but that applies only to events in which data or changes are written to an app.
NewCore contacted Grok Bot support on November 4. At the time, users had no way to turn off the automatic check-ins. Then, eight days later, Hoorvitch said, the Cursor dashboard, the administrative console behind Grok Bot, received an update. Under bot capabilities, a new toggle called proactive messages appeared. By default, it’s set to on. When a team admin sets it to off, bots no longer run check-ins on their own.
SpaceXSI representatives didn’t answer questions sent by email.

articles.title_orig: Lisa Cook lawyer signals Fed gov won't attend Trump committee's hearing
articles.title_zh: Lisa Cook lawyer signals Fed gov won't attend Trump committee's hearing
articles.content_orig:
Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook 's attorney on Tuesday gave the strongest signal yet that his client will not attend a hearing at the White House with a "committee of inquiry" investigating mortgage fraud allegations against Cook.
The committee established last month by President Donald Trump , who has previously tried to remove Cook from the central bank's board, is pretextual and poses a threat to the Fed, attorney Abbe Lowell wrote in a letter to presidential counsel Will Scharf.
"Governor Cook has no legal obligation to participate in an unfair hearing — and indeed, has a duty to the Federal Reserve to decline to participate in any proceeding that would undermine the institution's unique status and independence," Lowell wrote in the letter, which is dated Monday and was made public Tuesday.
The latest correspondence came nearly two weeks after the White House committee delayed its proposed hearing with Cook to Dec. 14 from Nov. 5. Lowell said that any hearing with Cook could not take place until at least December because of conflicts with her Fed duties.
While Lowell had raised strong concerns from the outset about the legitimacy of the committee, he initially said Cook "welcomes the opportunity to present the facts so she can clear her name."
But he has continued to cast doubts on both the committee's purpose and its composition of three executive branch officials, including National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett .
Lowell's tone sounded more hostile than ever in this week's letter, the first known to be sent by either party in the matter since the Republican Party's devastating losses in the midterm elections on Nov. 3.
He accused Scharf and the committee of seeking "only to manufacture 'cause' for a predetermined removal outcome."
Lowell highlighted two top concerns. First, he asserted that Hassett "is not competent to serve on any factfinding committee" because his prior comments about Cook "demonstrate that he has prejudged the issue."
Second, Lowell called it "fundamentally unfair" that the committee is demanding Cook hand over documents "immediately," while pledging to provide the governor with its own records just seven days before the hearing.
"Your and the Committee's failure to address these legitimate issues, over multiple weeks of back-and-forth correspondence, reinforces my prior observation: President Trump's decision to fire Governor Cook has already been made," Lowell wrote.
"Consequently, this Committee process appears to be a façade designed to obscure a predetermined decision to fire Governor Cook or to unreasonably manufacture a supposed 'adverse inference' if she does not participate in a process that does not comport with the requirements of a fair hearing," the lawyer wrote.
Lowell told Scharf that Cook would still be prepared to appear for a hearing if the White House "implements fair procedures." But the "ultimatums" Scharf gave in his last reply in early November "do not provide a productive path forward to enabling that participation," Lowell wrote.
The White House did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on Lowell's letter.
Trump, who frequently urges the Fed to lower interest rates, has long sought to fire Cook, an appointee of former President Joe Biden .
Cook, the first Black woman to serve on the Fed's Board of Governors, last voted to cut rates in December 2025, siding with the majority. The Fed unanimously voted to raise rates after its meeting in September.
Trump officials sent a criminal referral last year alleging Cook may have committed mortgage fraud by falsely claiming different properties as her primary residence in order to get more favorable terms. Cook adamantly denied wrongdoing, and, after Trump tried to fire her in August 2025, filed a lawsuit to block her removal.
The Supreme Court in June prevented Trump from firing Cook, but gave him a path to try again if additional legal steps were taken. In August, the White House told Cook it was reviving its efforts to fire her on mortgage-related grounds. In October, Trump signed a presidential memo establishing the committee of inquiry to investigate allegations that Cook lied on records related to "one or more mortgage instruments."
